10760-a-florida-sketch-book:
Bradford Torrey, a New England bird lover, published A Florida Sketch Book in 1894 after winter travels in the state. Its sketches run from the flat-woods near Jacksonville and the marsh beside the road to the beach at Daytona, the Hillsborough, the upper St. John's, and the St. Augustine road. Walks about Tallahassee and a Florida shrine complete the tour.

Torrey writes of birds, pines, and water with a naturalist's patience, finding beauty in a landscape newcomers called barren. His tone is gentle and observant. Readers get a charming record of Florida before the boom, when pine barrens and small towns set the scene.
11260-the-kiltartan-history-book:
Lady Gregory's Kiltartan History Book, illustrated by Robert Gregory and dedicated to history classes in the new university, retells Irish history in the plain speech of Kiltartan country people. Contents run from ancient times, Goban the builder, and the Danes through Clontarf, Cromwell in Connacht, the Famine, the Fenians, and Parnell, ending with the old age pension and a prophecy. Notes close the volume.

Gregory collected these stories from oral tradition, letting old women, tinkers, and neighbors tell history as they remembered it. The result is partisan and vivid, a people's history rather than a textbook's. For readers of the Irish revival, the book shows Gregory turning folklore into national narrative.
11493-the-blotting-book:
E. F. Benson's 1908 novel opens in Mrs. Assheton's house in Sussex Square, Brighton, where meals are punctual, rooms are never too hot or cold, and two quiet parlour-maids meet every want of a guest. Order rules the house like the solar system, with no fear of comets crossing its sky.

That calm breaks into darker matter, with a man worn to exhaustion, rain hushing him to sleep, and a stormy evening on the sea below. The title points to the blotter where private writing leaves its trace, and the story turns on what orderly lives hide.
11921-the-illustrated-london-reading-boo:
The Illustrated London Reading Book, printed and published at the office of the Illustrated London News, 198, Strand, appeared in a third edition with additions and corrections in 1851. An illustration shows Prince Albert in his robes as Chancellor of the University of Cambridge, a mark of the book's respectable, improving aims.

Designed for young readers and for schools, the reading book mixes short pieces of history, geography, science, and moral instruction with engravings. Its London origin shows in its selection and tone: a mid-Victorian miscellany meant to teach reading through interesting matter, rather than through dull exercises. To give children a picture of the wider world.
12216-the-pirates-own-book:
Charles Ellms published The Pirates Own Book in 1837, gathering authentic narratives of celebrated sea robbers for American readers. Ellms wrote for a public fascinated by piracy, and his preface warns that pirate crews were formed of desperadoes from every nation.

Lives follow Captain Condent, Blackbeard, and others through mutiny, capture, murder, and the plank, with scenes in the West Indies, the Indian Ocean, and off Africa. Ellms mixes court records, newspaper reports, and sailor yarns, and modern scholars check his facts with care. Still, the book fixed the pirate image for generations: buried treasure, black flags, and crews who lived by the maxim that dead men tell no tales.
12227-child-s-first-picture-book:
Child First Picture Book is a book of pictures with short captions for very young readers, printed with illustrations on nearly every page. The captions name and explain familiar machines and scenes in plain words.

Fire horses stand ready in stalls, and at the alarm gong the chains drop, collars clamp, and the engine rushes off at break-neck speed. An automobile fire engine follows, then trains, some made up to follow college boat races along river banks, and a train ferry. A circus coming to town closes the parade of sights. The book has little continuous prose, but its captions build a child vocabulary of work, speed, and spectacle.
12519-the-virginia-housewife-or-methodic:
Mrs. Mary Randolph's Virginia Housewife, or Methodical Cook, in an 1860 printing, is a classic American cookbook with a motto: method is the soul of management. Soups open the book, from asparagus, beef, gravy, veal, oyster, barley and pea to ochra, hare, catfish, onion and mock turtle of calf's head.

Beef, veal and other meats follow, with directions for curing, drying, corning, roasting, boiling and frying, plus beef à-la-mode, olives, fricando and steak pie. Randolph writes for a plantation household, practical and precise. The book preserves early Southern cooking in detail, and it remains a touchstone for food historians tracing American taste.
12584-phebe-her-profession-a-sequel-to-t:
Anna Chapin Ray's 1902 sequel, Phebe, Her Profession, follows Teddy's book with a new heroine's working life. Chapter one opens in Helena. A young man in a brown study meets a wee boy, a cherub in modern raiment, with sugary smears, a crumpled paper bag, a rusty hoop and a cudgel. The boy asks after everybody at the young man's house.

Phebe's profession, teaching or a kindred calling, gives the novel its centre, as young people, children and households cross in a New England setting. Ray writes in a warm, wholesome manner for girl readers. The book offers a gentle story of work, friendship and growing up, sequel to a popular girls' tale.
13188-putnam-s-word-book:
Louis A. Flemming's Putnam's Word Book, copyright 1913, is a practical aid to exact and varied vocabulary, first titled Synonyms, Antonyms, and Associated Words. It opens with a list of abbreviations, from adjectives and adverbs to botany, chemistry, civil law, and military terms. The main body is alphabetical, word by word, with synonyms and near kin.

Entries give, for example, disobedience as contumacy, defiance, and insubordination, and disorder as confusion, jumble, tumult, and Bedlam. Later pages run from outskirt to overbearing, with shades from haughty to imperious. The book is a writer's tool, meant to sit beside the desk and sharpen a sentence without a trip to a full dictionary.
13344-the-moral-picture-book:
A small illustrated book for children, built around John Cooper, an only child living with his parents in a cottage by a village green. John plays with his dog Carlo and with Tom Jones, who tempts him to skip school for a long walk by a winding stream. The walk, and what follows, becomes a lesson in obedience and its costs.

Later stories follow John away from home, his ageing parents praying for a son who may be killed or wounded in war, and other kind acts repaid in turn. Sarah Jenkins and Harry help a tired old man on his way to a sick soldier son. Simple tales, pictures, and prayer frame each moral point for young readers and their teachers.
13669-the-new-dr-price-cookbook:
The New Dr. Price Cook Book of 1921, for use with Dr. Price's Phosphate Baking Powder from Chicago, promises recipes of universal appeal, useful every meal every day the year through. Famous recipes are made more appealing by the powder, economising in eggs and other expensive ingredients, while new recipes suit beginners yet may add laurels to an expert's reputation.

Layer cake creams shortening and sugar, adds water drop by drop, stirs flour and baking powder sifted twice, and folds in stiff egg whites before baking in two greased pans. Cream soups follow a common foundation: pea soup from mashed green peas, celery rubbed through a sieve, potato soup strained with parsley, and corn soup from a can. The book is advertising cookery, practical and thrifty.
14-the-1990-cia-world-factbook:
Officials who need quick facts on any country turn to a yearly reference from the Central Intelligence Agency. The 1990 World Factbook covers 249 nations, dependent areas, and other entities. Entries were built for United States government use.

Each entry follows a set pattern on geography, people, government, and economy. The volume also lists oceans and disputed areas alongside states. Its snapshot predates the Soviet collapse, freezing a world on the edge of change. Researchers still use it as a baseline for that year. Historians now pair it with later editions to measure how fast borders and regimes changed.
14127-a-kindergarten-story-book:
Jane L. Hoxie gathered stories told to thousands of children in kindergartens from Boston to Pittsburgh, publishing them for ages four to six. A tenth edition from Milton Bradley in 1916 keeps the simple, varied set that teachers had already tested in classrooms. Short tales, rhymes, and retellings suit an evening story hour, the happiest memory of the author's own childhood.

Cumulative tales teach listening through repetition. A child sends staff, hatchet, fire, and water in turn to fetch a stubborn kid home by moonlight. Cinderella tries the glass slipper before her sisters' protests fail, and two sisters call for lost Indra in a forest hut. Gentle morals, clear speech, and room for voices and gestures mark every piece. Parents and teachers still find here a model of early storytelling: brief, musical, and built for young ears.
15456-mcguffey-s-eclectic-spelling-book:
This revised edition of McGuffey's Eclectic Spelling Book, in the Eclectic Educational Series, preserves the famous schoolbook's plan while updating its marks. The old system of numerals called superiors, used to show pronunciation, gives way to Webster's diacritical marks. Spelling, pronunciation, and syllabication follow the latest Webster's Unabridged Dictionary.

Exercises cover each distinctive mark, and the transcriber notes that only accent emphasis survives in plain text, with full graphics in other formats. A playful note asks whether readers still recall how to spell pharmacopoeia or Winnipiseogee, once sixth-grade fare. The speller shows American schooling around 1900: drill, accent, and clear rules, in a book that shaped how generations learned to spell and say words.
15661-the-golden-goose-book:
Four classic fairy tales for young readers, retold and drawn by L. Leslie Brooke and first printed in London in 1905. Brooke pairs each tale with colour and black-and-white drawings, so the pictures carry much of the humour and charm. The tales come from older folk sources, told here in short, clear prose. Frederick Warne and Company issued the book for children and for reading aloud.

The title tale follows a youngest son mocked as a simpleton, whose kindness to a small grey man earns him a golden goose. The Three Bears, the Three Little Pigs, and Tom Thumb complete the set. Each tale turns on wit, manners, and a fair reward for good conduct. Read together, they offer a compact shelf of tales that children can follow, retell, and enjoy on their own.
16448-jewel-s-story-book:
Clara Louise Burnham follows the young heroine Jewel through eighteen short chapters in this 1904 book for children. Jewel charms the grown-ups around her, from housekeeper Mrs. Forbes to Mr. Evringham, with tales, gifts, and small acts of grace. Chapters range from a phone call and a broker's office to a quest flower, a talking doll, and a birthday.

The stories are gentle and warm, with a moral glow but no heavy preaching. Burnham writes for children who loved Jewel in earlier books, and each chapter can be read alone at bedtime. The book gives a sweet picture of Edwardian family life through a child's bright eyes.
1662-the-1997-cia-world-factbook:
The 1997 CIA World Factbook gathers country profiles for every state and territory known to American intelligence in that year, from Afghanistan to the Arctic Ocean and beyond. An introduction, a brief history of basic intelligence, and notes and definitions explain the fields, and a guide to profiles sets out categories and subfields.

Each entry covers geography, people, government, economy, communications, and defence, in the Factbook's compact, standard form. The volume is a snapshot of the world in 1997, just after the Cold War's end. It is a useful reference for historians, and a period record of how one government saw the globe.
16637-sleep-book:
Leolyn Louise Everett collected poems of slumber in this 1910 Sleep-Book, printed in only three hundred and twenty copies on handmade paper. The opening poem bids an over-anxious heart rest, quiet wild dreams, and let night take the sleeper to herself. Coleridge on sleep's softly-breathing god and a trickling stream to lull slumber follow.

The anthology gathers short lyrics for bedtime reading, dedicated to Ethel du Fre Houston, who brought dream beauty into many lives. The tone is gentle throughout. Readers seeking verse for the night will find a rare, lovely little book, made to be read slowly before sleep.
17104-the-rocket-book:
Peter Newell's 1912 picture book starts in a basement, where Fritz, the janitor's boy, lights a stray rocket. The rocket shoots up through the whole house, flat by flat. Each spread shows the mishap it causes: a smashed catsup bottle, a lost wig, and a burst bubble. Verse on each page tells what the blast does next.

Newell's joke is the chain itself: one small act of mischief wrecks a whole building in order, from cellar to roof. Children love the climb, the crash, and the neat pictures that track the rocket's path. It is a word-light, laugh-loud classic of early picture books, built for reading aloud and looking close.
17254-the-slant-book:
Peter Newell's 1910 Slant Book tells, in verse and pictures, of Bobby and a runaway go-cart on a steep hill. The book itself is cut on a slant, so the hill runs through its pages. Bobby's cart breaks away, the nurse screams, and Bobby laughs as he speeds down, past a cop, a Greek pushcart man, a hydrant, and a farmer's wife with eggs.

Newell's joke is physical: the slant shape makes the downhill rush real to the eye and hand. Children love the crash, the splash, and Bobby's snipped button as he sails past the cop. It is a word-light, laugh-loud picture book classic, built for reading aloud and for tipping downhill with Bobby.
17978-leaves-from-a-field-note-book:
J. H. Morgan wrote Leaves from a Field Note-Book in 1916, printed in London by Macmillan, with a dedication to General Macready of the British Expeditionary Force. Morgan served as a Home Office commissioner with the force in France, and his notes give the war from just behind the front.

Leaves run from the base, with Bobs Bahadur and the base depot, to the front, with the two Richebourgs, idols of the cave, and Stokes's act. A court scene, with a fine of twenty francs, shows war's odd, human side. Morgan writes with wit and warmth. It is a vivid, humane war book, full of soldiers, courts, and daily life.
180-the-1994-cia-world-factbook:
The Central Intelligence Agency's 1994 Factbook continues the yearly survey of states and territories. Country entries follow the familiar pattern: geography, people, government, economy, communications, and defense forces. Search marks let readers jump straight to a country and section.

The edition notes purchase and subscription routes through the Superintendent of Documents, plus microfiche and diskette formats. Afghanistan again opens the alphabetical run. The 1994 volume records a post-Cold War map still settling into new borders. It serves as a detailed reference for that year. Scholars use the 1994 volume to date border changes in the former Soviet space.
18071-the-spinster-book:
Myrtle Reed wrote The Spinster Book, printed in New York and London by G. P. Putnam's Sons, copyright 1901 and reprinted through 1907. Reed, author of Lavender and Old Lace, here writes with wit on men, women, and love.

Chapters run from notes on men and concerning women to the philosophy of love, the lost art of courtship, the natural history of proposals, and an inquiry into marriage. Widowers, widows, and the consolations of spinsterhood close the set. Reed writes with light, sharp humor. It is a delightful, period book of essays, best for readers who like wit on love.
18344-the-song-of-sixpence-picture-book:
Walter Crane's picture book gathers three favorites for children: Sing a Song of Sixpence, Princess Belle Etoile, and An Alphabet of Old Friends. Crane supplied the original colored designs, and the volume adds a preface and other embellishments. John Lane published it in London and New York, with Crane's preface dated at Kensington in September 1909.

Each couplet of Sing a Song of Sixpence gets its own picture, so the nursery rhyme unfolds page by page in color. Princess Belle Etoile brings a fairy tale, and the alphabet gives old friends their letters. Children get a book made to be looked at slowly: rhyme, tale, and alphabet bound in one bright volume by a leading illustrator of the age.
18561-the-ontario-readers-third-book:
The Ontario Minister of Education authorized this third reader, published in Toronto by the T. Eaton Company, entered in 1909 under the Parliament of Canada. It gathers poems, stories, and passages for schoolchildren, with thanks to Kipling, Newbolt, Dickens, Roberts, and many other writers whose work appears here.

Early pages give Carlyle's To-day, a beggar tale, a lark and rook poem, and Dickens on the Pickwick Club on the ice. The book teaches reading through short, varied pieces, each chosen for a young reader's ear, and stands as a record of what Ontario schoolchildren read in the early twentieth century.
18674-a-chinese-wonder-book:
Norman Hinsdale Pitman wrote this wonder book at New York in 1919, with pictures by Li Chu-Tang. It holds fifteen Chinese tales. They run from the Golden Beetle, or why the dog hates the cat, and the Great Bell to the Strange Tale of Doctor Dog, How Footbinding Started, and the Talking Fish. Later tales bring Bamboo and the Turtle, the Nodding Tiger, Princess Kwan-Yin, and Lu-San, Daughter of Heaven.

The opening tale follows Widow Wang and her son Ming-li through a hard winter, a fallen roof, sickness, and lost work. Pitman retells the tales in plain, warm English for young readers. The book gives a friendly first taste of Chinese folk story.
18702-the-ontario-readers-fourth-book:
This school reader, authorized by Ontario's Minister of Education and entered in 1909, gathers poems and prose for classroom reading. Toronto's T. Eaton Company published it as the Fourth Book of the Ontario Readers series.

Its contents mix British classics with Canadian pieces. Kipling, Tennyson, Shakespeare, and Dickens stand beside Roberts on Canada, Parkman on Wolfe and Montcalm, and Haight on country life in Canada in the thirties. Bible passages, ballads, and tales like Scrooge's Christmas and The Ancient Mariner give teachers matter for reading aloud and study. The book shows what Ontario schoolchildren of the day were expected to read and recite.
19207-the-firelight-fairy-book:
Henry Beston wrote this 1919 Firelight Fairy Book, with pictures by Maurice E. Day. It gathers fairy tales for fireside reading, with a glossary of hard words such as cataplasm, doggerel, halberdiers, and seneschal. The tales mix wonder, humour, and moral lessons in old-style prose.

A prince pushes a boat into a river, shoots through a cavern into the heart of the earth, and wakes on a black, glassy underground ocean beneath a strange golden glow. Giant pillars and twisted columns frame his path. Young readers get enchanting fairy tales of quests, magic, and brave princes.
19392-the-little-tea-book:
Arthur Gray compiled this 1903 Little Tea Book, with pictures by George W. Hood. It follows his Over the Black Coffee. Colley Cibber's praise opens it, calling tea a soft, sober, sage liquid. Cibber calls it a tongue-running, heart-opening cordial. The book gathers verse, lore, and praise of tea as the drink of the world.

Versifiers hail tea over coffee, calling it the crystal stream above flowing mud. They sing its worth in failing words. Doctors quarrel over its merits. Foes cite roast beef, strong beer, and sturgeon as better fare. Readers get a charming anthology for tea lovers, witty, learned, and fond.
19879-five-pebbles-from-the-brook:
Five Pebbles from the Brook examines the grounds of Christianity. Its subtitle states the method: comparing the New Testament with the Old. The author pictures scripture as an edifice on a foundation. The Law and the Prophets are that foundation, he argues. If the later books irreconcilably clash with the older revelation, their authority falls. The argument proceeds text against text, closely.

George Bethune English wrote this attack in the early republic. He had traveled in Egypt and served in its army. His pebbles are five arguments slung at orthodoxy, David-style. Deist and freethinking pamphlets like his stirred American pulpits. The book survives as evidence of that fight. It is combative, learned, and unmistakably of 1813.
1995-united-states-congressional-address:
A directory for citizens who want to write to their government, drawn from the Project Gutenberg listing of the United States Congress for 1995. The front matter argues for paper over electronics: a letter carries the most impact, then a fax, then a call, then an email. It gives the Judiciary committee chairs of both chambers as first targets, with room numbers, phone, and fax.

The main body lists members of Congress with their Washington office buildings and room numbers, plus standard mailing forms for senators and representatives. The White House addresses of President Bill Clinton and Vice President Al Gore appear with early public email addresses. As a snapshot it preserves how Americans reached Congress just before the web took over constituent mail.
2016-the-1998-cia-world-factbook:
This reference volume, prepared by the United States Central Intelligence Agency, surveys every country and territory known in 1998, from Afghanistan to the Arctic Ocean. Entries give geography, people, government, economy, and communications in compact form. The Factbook began as a government handbook, and its yearly editions track a world changing fast.

Maps and graphics from the print edition are absent here, and some tables may not line up neatly, but the facts remain intact. As a snapshot of the world at the end of the twentieth century, it serves students, researchers, and curious readers alike. Country entries follow the same order throughout, so a reader can compare any two nations side by side.
20652-ring-o-roses-a-nursery-rhyme-pictu:
L. Leslie Brooke illustrated Ring o' Roses, a nursery rhyme picture book, with pictures in color and in black and white. Brooke's drawings for children's classics were among the best of their age. The rhymes here are the first poems of the nursery.

Here is the finger rhyme every child learns. This little pig went to market, this little pig stayed at home, and this little pig had roast beef. This little pig had none, and the last cried wee, wee, wee, all the way home. Brooke's pigs act out the rhyme with comic charm.
20830-the-good-housekeeping-marriage-boo:
California students asked for a course in marriage relations, and a New York paper took note. The Good Housekeeping Marriage Book, from 1938, grew from that fresh demand. Its pages gather counsel from men and women who wrote on married life.

Courtship, money, sex, in-laws, and children all get frank, plain treatment. Good Housekeeping lent its trusted name to guide young couples of the day. The book marks a shift toward open, expert talk on marriage. Readers can see what counted as wise counsel on the eve of the Second World War, in middle-class American terms.
20952-a-jolly-jingle-book:
A little red man in a little red house with ivory gates stars in A Jolly Jingle-Book. He will talk and laugh at all you do, the riddle rhyme warns. Luther H. Cary's 1913 book of jingles dares children to name that red man.

Rhymes, riddles, and tongue play fill the book for young readers at home. Its verses beg to be read aloud, chanted, and guessed at in turns. Such jingle books fed the nursery trade in cheerful, harmless fun. The red man, your own tongue, gives the game away to sharp children, who then delight in springing it on others.
21007-the-bird-study-book:
Birds and spring feel like one word, says T. Gilbert Pearson in The Bird Study Book. Wild song, flashing wings, and mad dashes through thickets all spring from mating fire. His 1917 book opens on that riot of the breeding season.

Pearson, a founder of the Audubon movement, teaches how to watch birds with care. Nests, migration, food, and protection fill his plain, keen chapters. He urges readers to guard birds, not just name them on lists. The book helped turn bird study into a mass American pastime, binoculars in hand and notebook ready at dawn.
21469-the-mate-of-the-lily-or-notes-from:
Harry Musgrave ships as an apprentice officer in W. H. G. Kingston's The Mate of the Lily. His father, Captain Musgrave, never came home from his last voyage, leaving his mother near destitute. Her brother Jack, mate of the Lily, steps in to support the family.

The Lily seeks a return cargo in the Java seas, where clues point to the lost captain. Storms, a volcano, grounding, and pirate attacks block the search. Near the end they find the captain alive, though sunk in despair. News of home revives him, and suspense holds the tale tight to the last.
21574-the-poacher-or-joseph-rushbrook:
Joseph Rushbrook's tale opens on a blustering November night in 1812 in Captain Marryat's The Poacher. Three men reel out of an alehouse, two half-carrying the third between them. Chapter one, Marryat warns, holds more ale than argument.

Rushbrook's poaching sets him against keepers, law, and his own better hopes. The book, Marryat's eighteenth, appeared in 1841 after his great sea tales. Village life, crime, and conscience get equal weight in the telling. Marryat knew the world of game laws from the inside, and his poacher is no stage villain but a full, flawed man.
21874-the-bay-and-padie-book:
Australian children sing through this 1917 book of kiddie songs by Furnley Maurice, with pictures by Vera Hamilton and Cyril Dobbs. Bay and Padie are small boys whose world holds trains, trams, sparrows, ponies, and grubs. The Shadow Show lists the wonders: aeroplanes, paper darts, woodmen's carts, and barking pups that knock the postman off his bike. Oh, what a lot of lots of things for little boys to see, the chorus runs.

Maurice thanks Sydney papers for leave to reprint pieces like Kitchen Lullaby and Little Boys. The book ran to a second edition within months, wholly printed in Australia. Its slang and sunshine are pure period Australia. Grown readers will find their grandparents' nursery world preserved in rhyme.
21914-the-woggle-bug-book:
Mr. H. M. Woggle-Bug, T. E., takes a walk down an American main street in L. Frank Baum's Woggle-Bug Book of 1905. The initials mean Highly Magnified and Thoroughly Educated, titles earned in the Land of Oz. Separated from his Oz companions, the giant insect has four hands and time hanging heavy on all of them. He marches with an air of importance, proud of his learning.

Ike Morgan's pictures show the Bug's queer figure, which he himself never suspects. In America his Oz education proves less remarkable than he hopes. Baum builds the joke gently: vanity in a frock coat, six feet of it. The book is a short, sunny offshoot of the Oz tales, made for readers who wanted one more visit with its oddest scholar.
21935-prince-prigio-from-his-own-fairy-b:
Prince Prigio of Pantouflia is too clever for his own good in Andrew Lang's fairy tale from his own invented book. Lang confesses in his preface that the famous colored Fairy Books were gathered from old tales, not made up by him. This one he did invent, with help from Pantouflia's historical papers. Pantouflia's kings descend from a Greek family that dodged the Crusades. Their crest is a dormouse asleep on a green field.

Prigio, blessed or cursed with magic gifts and a too-logical mind, must learn what cleverness cannot do. Lang writes the tale as a sly lesson in the limits of cleverness, dressed as pure fun. Pantouflia later got a second visit in Prince Ricardo. The humor still sparkles for grown readers as much as children.
22197-the-goody-naughty-book:
Sarah Cory Rippey wrote The Goody-Naughty Book in 1913 to teach small children their manners through stories. Its full title promises the goody side and the naughty side of child life. In one tale, little Rose-Red is comforted in her mother's arms after a quarrel. Ruthie is probably sorry now, her mother says, and Rose-Red must be ready to forgive when the apology comes.

Each short story pairs a fault with its gentle cure. Table manners, temper, truthfulness, and kindness all take their turn. The language is simple and the morals are spoken aloud by mothers. Such books lined the nursery shelves of progressive homes before child psychology changed the fashion.
22231-peak-and-prairie-from-a-colorado-s:
Anna Fuller gathered Peak and Prairie from a Colorado sketch-book in 1894. Fuller warns that her sketches are little more than hints caught by a single observer. Her field is narrow, but she promises it offers unusual variety. The health resort she calls Springtown stands at the centre, drawing many kinds of people into one small place.

Invalids, miners, tourists, and ranch folk cross in her sketches. Pike's Peak country gave Fuller her material, as it did in her earlier novel. She writes with humour and a traveller's quick sympathy. The book belongs to the local-colour movement that mapped America's regions for eastern readers, and Colorado Springs lives in it.
22335-harrison-s-new-nursery-picture-boo:
Harrison's New Nursery Picture Book offered children pictures and short pieces in one volume. Its list of plates shows what young readers were shown. Robinson Crusoe appears again and again in the illustrations.

Crusoe is cast on an uninhabited island in one picture. In others he finds a footprint and fires at attackers. Friday stands beside him in another plate. Other pictures show Edwin on his new rocking-horse and May-day amusements. A visit to an Indian juggler adds exotic flavor. Picture books like this shaped early reading. They mixed adventure, morals, and play in pages made to be looked at first.
22495-the-new-pun-book:
The New Pun Book, copyrighted in 1906 by Carey-Stafford, collects jokes built on wordplay. Each entry is a short exchange ending in a pun. The humor is quick, mild, and made for reading aloud.

He's a professional grafter, one joke announces of a nurseryman. Another asks what Fatty Schultz the butcher weighs: meat. A hardware sign reading cast iron sinks draws a knowing nod. Everyone, the joker says, is already wise to that fact. How are you today gets the answer, oh, I can't kick. Joke books like this filled railway journeys and parlor evenings. Readers get Edwardian humor in its lightest, groaning form.
22582-harrison-s-amusing-picture-and-poe:
Harrison's Amusing Picture and Poetry Book is a children's book of light verse paired with pictures. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its poems are short, rhymed, and built for young readers, with animals and everyday scenes as their subjects.

One sample poem speaks in a child's voice about a kind donkey that carries a sack to market and lets the rider sit on its back all the way. The verses promise gratitude and a handful of grass for the good-natured animal. Books of this kind mixed mild moral lessons with simple fun. Modern readers will find a gentle sample of the rhymes once read aloud in nurseries and early classrooms.
22825-the-smoker-s-year-book:
Verse carries The Smoker's Year Book of 1908, a light almanac that walks through the calendar. Its April poem gives the month a personality. Lady April appears as the spoilt child of the year, her tears melting old Winter's heart, then turning to tease Spring until Spring grows chilly and cross.

Month follows month in that playful register, mixing weather lore, jokes, and short poems for readers who smoked. The book belongs to the era's flood of novelty year books, made to sit on a desk and amuse in spare minutes. Little in it aims at weight. Its interest now is as a piece of everyday print culture, cheerful, disposable, and carefully preserved here all the same.
23302-a-flower-book:
Eden Coybee and Nellie Benson made this flower book for children, published in London as one of the Dumpy Books for Children. Small, cloth-bound, and bright, it belongs to a series that also offered cautionary stories, bad families, and schoolboy tales.

The book pairs short flower texts with pictures for young readers learning plant names and nature's charms. As a Dumpy Book, it was made to fit small hands and to be carried, read, and loved to pieces. Small cloth binding suits little hands, so the book travels well to gardens. The Windflower steps forward boldly, banner raised, telling her sisters that tears dry and give place to smiles.
23336-the-tiny-story-book:
Made for the youngest readers, this small story book offers short, plain tales of home life, each paired with a picture. A child visits a three year old cousin named Alice, plays at mothers with dolls, and rocks her small charge to sleep after tea.

Other tales follow a brother who sails away to sea, with his trunk packed and his kin waving from the shore. The sentences stay short, the scenes stay close to a child's day, and the morals stay gentle. Grown readers reading aloud will find a mild, old style primer in story form, built to teach kind conduct through play rather than through rules.
23353-a-horse-book:
Number ten in the Dumpy Books for Children, this small picture book offers short pieces about horses for young readers. Plain text and portraits of horses share the pages, in the same pocket size format as its sister volumes on cats, flowers, and other pets.

The book suits a child meeting horses for the first time: what they look like, how they move, and how people keep and ride them. Its charm lies in brevity and in the pictures, which let a small reader point, name, and ask. Grown readers will note the old style charm of the series, made to be carried, thumbed, and read again.
23407-the-tiny-picture-book:
George W. Hobbs of Charlestown printed this tiny picture book of short verses and pictures for very small children. Apples hang round, bright, and red on a green old tree. A naughty boy who tries to steal one falls and is left a cripple, a stern warning in a few lines.

Other verses praise hoop and top, bat and ball over rough play. They urge a boy to heed the school bell and keep every rule, and show a kind cat catching mice and washing her fur. The rhymes stay short and plain, each with a picture to point at. Parents reading aloud will find a mild, old fashioned moral primer, where good conduct earns praise and mischief earns a fall.
23598-little-bo-peep-a-nursery-rhyme-pic:
Leslie Brooke made this nursery rhyme picture book, printed by Frederick Warne in London and New York, with Little Bo Peep leading the set. Bo Peep has lost her sheep and cannot tell where to find them, so she leaves them alone to come home with tails behind them.

She falls asleep and dreams she hears them bleating, then wakes to find it a joke, for they still flee. She takes her little crook to seek them and finds them indeed, though it makes her heart bleed, for they left all their tails behind. Ring o' roses and a little man follow, each rhyme with a picture. Small children will love Brooke's drawings and the familiar rhymes, told with a gentle, old fashioned charm.
23673-the-st-gregory-hymnal-and-catholic:
The St. Gregory Hymnal and Catholic Choir Book gathers the old Latin hymns sung by Catholic choirs and congregations, with music and words arranged for use in church. Its pages hold the chant and hymn repertory that generations of schoolchildren sang from choir lofts, often standing near great organ pipes that stretched from floor to ceiling.

For singers and musicians today, the book serves as a source for those Latin hymns. Many are remembered only by a few words, yet a simple search of its text can recover a full hymn. It preserves a living piece of Catholic musical life: the melodies, verses, and order of singing that shaped worship before newer hymnals replaced them.
24083-every-man-his-own-poet-or-the-insp:
An Oxford writer calling himself a Newdigate Prizeman published this satirical handbook in 1872. It pretends that poetry can be cooked up from recipes, and offers step-by-step formulas for the fashionable verse of its day. Each chapter takes aim at a different style then filling the magazines.

Readers get recipes for an ordinary love poem, a pathetic marine poem, an epic in the manner of Tennyson, and poems after Matthew Arnold, Robert Browning, William Morris, and Lord Byron. The joke lands because the formulas fit so well: the book shows how easily a popular style can be copied once its tricks are named.
24125-a-little-book-for-a-little-cook:
Pillsbury published this small cookbook for children in Minneapolis in 1905, with copyright held by L. P. Hubbard. Its directions are plain and firm. Always use Pillsbury's Best Flour. Sift flour twice for cakes. Make all measures level with the edge of a knife. Use the same cups and spoons through one recipe. Read the whole recipe before setting out tools and goods.

A note to the modern reader in this reissue adds updated methods, such as spooning flour lightly into the cup without sifting, and gives fresh times for bread, biscuits, and gingerbread. The book keeps its old-fashioned charm for young cooks learning real kitchen habits. Readers get a nostalgic first cookbook, short, clear, and meant to be used.
24210-deerbrook:
Harriet Martineau wrote this novel in 1839, after her travels in America, alongside her book on Toussaint l'Ouverture. It gives a close view of upper middle class families in the mid nineteenth century, people who speak to kin in polite, even over-polite terms no modern family would use. For that reason, though not meant as such, the book stands as a true social document.

It opens with a town-bred traveler admiring a neat white house in rich country. The house may sit in a shrubbery, on a sunny common, or in a nook between hills. He dreams of dewy mornings, bright autumn lanes, and frosty winter days by the fire. Mr. Grey's house draws just such speculation. Readers get a village novel of manners, money, and reputation.
2435-the-crimson-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang's Crimson Fairy Book gathers tales from many lands, from Russian forests to Hungarian plains, in the colorful series that taught Victorian children the world's stories. The volume includes tales of clever youngest sons, enchanted princesses, and talking beasts, all told in Lang's plain, brisk style. The crimson binding marked it as one of the later, richer fairy books.

The collection's variety is its strength: no two tales come from quite the same tradition. Children and folklore lovers still enjoy its breadth. It stands as a classic of the fairy book series.
24387-the-community-cook-book:
This practical cook book was sold by the Class of Willing Workers of the Winter Street Baptist Church in Haverhill, Massachusetts. It claims to represent the best cookery found in any intelligent, progressive American community. One person and her needs were kept in mind through compiling and revising: the average American woman, to whom the book is dedicated. Its third edition dates to 1916, copyrighted in 1914 by Powell and White of Cincinnati.

Contents run from bread, biscuits, rolls, and pastry through cereals, soups, fish, and salads to meat, eggs, vegetables, and desserts. Cake, fruits, pickles and preserves, candies, miscellaneous dishes, and beverages follow, with definitions of foreign terms and an index. It opens with bread, the staff of life, and baking powder biscuits. Readers get a church community's cookery, plain and useful.
24560-the-jingle-book:
Carolyn Wells wrote this book of nonsense verse, published by Macmillan in 1901 with pictures by Oliver Herford. It opens with a tutor who plays the flute and teaches piping to two young pipers. The two ask him whether piping itself, or teaching pipers, is the harder task.

Later jingles offer two old kings, a day dream, a club, a puzzled poet, and a serious question, all in bouncing rhyme. Wells and Herford make a merry pair, words and pictures matching in wit. Young readers, and adults who love wordplay, will enjoy this bright book of rhymes meant to be read aloud and laughed over.
24593-the-oriental-story-book:
G. P. Quackenbos translated these tales from the German of Wilhelm Hauff, and D. Appleton published them at New York in 1855 with pictures by J. W. Orr. The book opens with The Caravan, and an introduction tells of Queen Phantasie, who ruled a distant kingdom where the sun never set on everlasting green gardens.

Hauff's tales follow merchants, caliphs, and travellers through the East, with magic, disguise, and moral turns. Quackenbos inscribes the volume to a friend of New Orleans, in memory of happy hours over the German classics. Young readers get a bright collection of Eastern wonder tales, in the storyteller's tradition of the Arabian Nights.
24609-the-motor-car-dumpy-book: T. W. H. Crosland wrote this tiny picture book, number 32 in the Dumpy Books for Children, published at London in 1904 with colour pictures by J. R. Monsell. In short captions it tells how travel changed. First an old gentleman walked before steam carriages waving a red flag. Then a noisy traction engine followed at four miles an hour. Then the motor car arrived, travelling forty miles an hour.
24624-the-red-romance-book:
Andrew Lang edited this Red Romance Book, published by Longmans, Green at London and New York in 1921. Its preface, What Romances Are, tells of a poor lonely boy in a great house who stole into the library and sobbed over Polexander, a huge dull book of eight hundred pages. Lang's book offers romances of a livelier kind.

Its stories, drawn from many lands and ages, include tales of knights, outlaws, and adventurers, among them Gunnar's meeting with Hallgerda. Lang's colour fairy and romance books delighted generations of children. Young readers get a rich collection of romantic tales, chosen by a master anthologist.
25-the-1991-cia-world-factbook:
A year later, the Central Intelligence Agency issued its 1991 survey of the world. The World Factbook for 1991 keeps the same official pattern as its predecessor. Country entries run from Afghanistan onward in alphabetical order.

Sections cover geography, people, government, economy, and communications for each state and territory. Data came from census, defense, state, and intelligence sources. The 1991 edition catches the Soviet Union in its final months. It serves as a dated but detailed record of a shifting world. Later editions would show a new map, making this volume a useful before-and-after marker.
251-1995-united-states-congressional-add:
Citizens who want Congress to listen need addresses, and this 1995 book supplies them. The United States Congressional Address Book lists senators and representatives with office rooms and phone numbers. A note advises that a letter beats a fax, a fax beats a call, and a call beats email.

Judiciary chairs Orrin Hatch and Henry Hyde head the practical guidance, with their Washington offices given. The Gutenberg file trims column spacing and adds White House and other persons of interest. The book captures Congress in 1995 for historians and letter writers. It is a plain, useful civic tool.
25190-a-tramp-s-notebook:
Morley Roberts's Tramp's Note-Book, published in London in 1904, collects travel sketches from a wandering writer's life. Roberts had roamed widely, and his notes range from a watch-night service in San Francisco to Portuguese sketches and a boy from Pondicherry.

Later pieces visit R. L. Stevenson, Cape Town, Mafeking, the Fraser River, and British Columbia, and record a talk with President Kruger. Corsica, the Matterhorn, a socialist congress, and Texas animals follow. The book reads as a tramp's diary, curious about people everywhere and loyal to none of the usual tourist routes.
25462-little-folks-handy-book:
Lina Beard and Adelia B. Beard teach children to make toys and amusements from cheap stuff. Their chapters cover paper building cards, berry-basket toys, straw and paper furniture, and a newspaper boat that sails on real water. Paper jewelry, spool toys, envelope toys, clothespin toys, and scrap-books follow, with twig people and visiting-card houses.

One favourite is the transformation scrap-book, whose pages are cut a third of the way down so heads, bodies, and legs mix into funny figures. The book also shows how to play Indians in newspaper costumes. Charles Scribner's Sons published it in 1910, with pictures by the authors, who warn that all its material is original to them.
25553-my-flower-pot-child-s-picture-book:
Rufus Merrill of Concord, New Hampshire, publishes this small child's picture book, opening with a verse on flowers as fairy things sent to bless and teach purity. Pictures face short verses throughout, in the simple style of early American children's books.

Verses praise flowers kissed by showers in garden bowers, birds singing in deep valleys, and minds roving to kind thoughts. The flower-pot gives the book its title and its homely centre: a child, flowers, and pictures together, meant to please the eye and stir gentle feeling in very young readers.
25631-a-poetical-cook-book:
This poetical cook book opens with Owen Meredith's verses on cooks and dining: man may live without poetry, music, art, conscience, heart, friends, or books, but civilised man cannot live without cooks. Knowledge may grieve, hope may deceive, and passion may pine, yet no man can live without dining.

Recipes in verse follow, turning kitchen work into rhyme and humour for readers who cook and readers who merely eat. Footnotes in the text keep both symbol and numbered markers, with corrections listed at the end, preserving the book's Victorian print quirks for modern readers.
25658-daisy-ashford-her-book:
Daisy Ashford gathers her remaining novels in this book. She wrote The Young Visiters as a child. Spelling and punctuation errors are kept intact, except for three clear printer's errors listed at the end. Titles were written on separate pages, then repeated, and the repeats are omitted here.

Missing letters appear as asterisks, and dialogue often lacks final punctuation or a quotation mark, preserving the child's hand. On page 335, a chapter on Mr. Hose making enquiries begins with a small letter, a typical Ashford quirk. The collection lets readers enjoy a child author's novels exactly as she wrote them.
25914-the-khaki-kook-book:
Mary Kennedy Core gathers one hundred cheap and practical recipes, mostly from Hindustan, in this 1917 book printed for the author at Bareilly, India. The idea was born ten years before at Almora, a Himalayan station where deodar slopes hold the bungalows of European residents and snows tower above. One summer day Lilavate Singh made a tiffin of Hindustani food that won such praise the party planned a cook book on the spot.

Chapters cover savory dishes from other countries, split peas or dal, pickles and chutneys, and a catch all of most everything. Recipes use onion, tomato, and pepper cooked in oil till thick, then cold meat heated through, and a Spanish Welsh rarebit of onion, tomato soup, sharp cheese, pimentos, and mushrooms. The book is plain, thrifty, and full of Indian flavor.
26019-europa-s-fairy-book:
Joseph Jacobs restores and retells the fairy tales of Europe in Europa's Fairy Book, printed by Putnam in 1916 with pictures by John D. Batten. A grandfather's opening chat sets the tone: children beg for a tale, promise to be good and quiet, and learn that fairy tale time is no time at all. Jacobs dedicates the book to a long roll of granddaughters, Peggy, Madge, Pearl, Maggie, and many more.

Jacobs recalls writing a book years before for their mother May, with tales English children heard from mothers who heard them from mothers. One tale turns on a lazy man, a chicken eaten by a savage sow, and a landlord forced to hand over the sow with curses. The man walks the sow to another inn and asks room for them both. The book keeps old tales fresh for new children.
26068-the-bath-tatting-book:
P. P. teaches tatting in The Bath Tatting Book, printed by Emily Faithfull in London in 1865 for one shilling. Terms and directions open the book. A loop is written L, single stitches form two ways by shuttle over back or palm of hand, and two singles worked in turn make a double stitch. Reversing the order makes a reversed double, giving the work a right and a wrong side.

Patterns follow for doyleys and an imitation gymp, with ovals counted in doubles and loops, tied to foundation threads, drawn close, and repeated round circles. The book is a small, practical manual for a Victorian fancy art, precise in counts and plain in method, meant for hands learning lace by shuttle and thread.
26151-the-tapestry-book:
Helen Churchill Candee's 1912 survey traces woven wall hangings from antiquity to her own day, with four colour plates and ninety-nine black-and-white pictures. Chapters move from France and Flanders in the 1400s, through the high Gothic style and the Renaissance. They go on to Italy, the Gobelins factory, Beauvais, Aubusson, Savonnerie, and the English Mortlake works.

Practical chapters explain how tapestry is made. They show how to read borders and weavers' marks, and how to tell one shop or period from another. A full chapter covers the Bayeux Tapestry. Drawn from museum collections in New York, Chicago, Boston, and Washington, the book serves both as a history of the craft and as a guide for collectors and curious visitors.
26197-the-nursery-rhyme-book:
Andrew Lang edited this 1897 collection, with pictures by L. Leslie Brooke, for children who learn rhymes by heart before they can read. His preface recalls his own childhood box of tattered picture books, and how he learned to read without tears by picking out letters in Who Killed Cock Robin. He notes that some rhymes were printed three hundred years ago.

Grandmothers sang these songs to grandchildren for centuries, and Scottish knee-rides still passed them on by voice. The book names Old King Cole and sets King Arthur about 500 to 600 AD, so young readers meet history beside nonsense. It gathers the rhymes in one handsome volume, meant to be read aloud, remembered, and handed down again.
26209-the-golden-age-cook-book:
Henrietta Latham Dwight's 1898 cook book is built for readers who eat no meat. Its dedication speaks to all who strive to follow the Golden Rule in daily life. Opening pages quote Genesis on green herbs given for food, the command not to kill, and Daniel's trial of pulse and water.

Recipes that follow use vegetables, eggs, and grains in place of flesh. Tomatoes with egg, French carrots in brown sauce, and baked dishes with bread crumbs and butter show the range. The book blends moral argument with kitchen practice, and it stands as an early American guide to meatless cooking for health and conscience alike.
26323-the-suffrage-cook-book:
The Suffrage Cook Book, compiled by Mrs. L. O. Kleber for the Equal Franchise Federation of Western Pennsylvania, appeared at Pittsburgh in 1915. It is dedicated to Mrs. Henry Villard and Mrs. J. O. Miller. Its introduction treats cook books as old as printed books themselves, recalling cures, love charms, and lucky days tucked beside recipes in older volumes.

Later pages give plain, tested recipes, from egg bread scalded with boiling water to quick waffles beaten light with milk and flour. The book joins kitchen practice to a political cause, putting women's votes beside women's work. Readers get both a usable cook book and a snapshot of suffrage organizing in Pennsylvania on the eve of victory.
26374-the-cookery-blue-book:
The Cookery Blue Book, prepared by the Society for Christian Work of the First Unitarian Church in San Francisco and printed in 1891, calls itself tried and true. A Shakespeare epigraph on a cold dinner opens the collection, which then moves straight to soups. Bouillon soup simmers four pounds of diced beef in four quarts of water for six hours, skimmed with care so no grease clouds it.

Later recipes stuff tomatoes with chopped beets, bake cream potatoes in thin layers with butter and cream, and escallop cold sliced potatoes. The book reads as a community cook book, with church members sharing dishes that worked in their own kitchens. It offers plain, tested fare for family tables, without fuss or foreign airs.
26386-laboulaye-s-fairy-book:
French writer Édouard Laboulaye wrote the tales collected here, translated by Mary L. Booth with an introduction by Kate Douglas Wiggin. The volume gathers stories such as Yvon and Finette, The Castle of Life, Destiny, The Twelve Months, Swanda the Piper, and The Story of the Noses. Edward G. McCandlish supplied the pictures.

Wiggin opens by recalling a thick green book with gilt edges from her own youth, and the tales keep that old-fashioned charm. Kings, giants, talking beasts, and good counsel fill the pages, and each story turns on a choice, a kindness, or a fault repaid. Destiny himself appears at table in one tale, handing out gold to souls born that night.
27258-from-slave-to-college-president-be:
From Slave to College President, the life story of Booker T. Washington, in the Lives Worth Living series of popular biographies, opens with Wanted: A Man, the man found. Washington, the much-needed chief found at length, built distinguished work on behalf of his race at the great school whose story the book tells.

The era of freedom follows, with the realization that knowledge is power, as Washington rises from slavery to lead a college. The biography weighs public estimates of him, noting where praise runs exaggerated, and presents a life of labour, learning, and leadership for young readers of the series.
27321-fairy-book:
Sophie May's Fairy Book, published by Lee and Shepard in 1866 in the Little Prudy series and dedicated to little Bessie, gathers fairy tales from Cristobal to Wild Robin. The frontispiece shows Cristobal, and the introduction leads young readers into a world of enchantment.

By a lake shore, a water-kelpie sees a weeping lady and comes as a white-haired old man. He offers his kingdom under the waters, where streets are paved with red and white coral. She answers, I cannot go yet, thinking of her husband's kind words, though the kelpie returns each day with the same question, in May's gentle Victorian fairy tales.
27348-the-2007-cia-world-factbook:
The 2007 edition of the CIA World Factbook gathers country-by-country reference data, updated to 8 February 2007, in one large volume. Every country and location gets an entry built from the same set of fields. The book adds rank orders, maps, and appendixes for readers who want to compare nations side by side.

New work in this edition expands the capital entry with coordinates, time difference from coordinated universal time, and daylight saving notes. It adds a trafficking in persons entry plus a new appendix of weights and measures. Students, journalists, and general readers still use it as a quick first stop for basic facts about any country in the world.
27509-the-2006-cia-world-factbook:
The 2006 edition of the CIA World Factbook gives country-by-country reference data, updated to 19 December 2006. Its contents run from country listings and field listings to rank orders, appendixes, notes, and definitions.

Two changes mark this edition. Montenegro's successful secession referendum of May 2006 let it leave its union with Serbia, so the two Balkan countries are listed separately. The capital entry also grows, with coordinates, time difference from coordinated universal time, and daylight saving notes. A trafficking in persons entry joins the transnational issues category. A special note marks countries with multiple time zones.
27558-the-2003-cia-world-factbook:
The 2003 edition of the CIA World Factbook gives country-by-country reference data, updated to 18 December 2003. Its printed version pictures the world as it stood on 1 January 2003, with countries, field listings, rank orders, and appendixes.

New work in this edition adds a rank order page for highways, with downloadable tab-delimited files. It also adds four entries to the economy category of each country: natural gas production, consumption, exports, and imports. Students, journalists, and general readers can compare nations on the same fields, as in other editions. A transcriber's note tells readers to prefix a country name with an at-sign to search it.
27559-the-2004-cia-world-factbook:
The 2004 edition of the CIA World Factbook gives country-by-country reference data, updated to 10 February 2005. Its contents run from country listings and field listings to rank orders, appendixes, and notes and definitions.

New entities appear in this edition. The Sovereign Base Areas of Akrotiri and Dhekelia on Cyprus, administered by the United Kingdom as dependencies, join the listing. The European Union also appears as an Other entity at the end. Five new fields arrive too, including current account balance, public debt, and a refugees and internally displaced persons entry.
27560-the-2005-cia-world-factbook:
The 2005 edition of the CIA World Factbook gives country-by-country reference data, updated to 20 October 2005. Its contents run from country listings and field listings to rank orders, appendixes, and notes and definitions.

New entities appear this year. The Sovereign Base Areas of Akrotiri and Dhekelia on Cyprus, administered by the United Kingdom as dependencies, join the listing. The European Union also appears as an Other entity at the end, as it accrues more nation-like traits. Six new fields arrive too, including major infectious diseases and public debt. A fuller explanation of the European Union listing sits under its preliminary statement.
27602-the-true-story-book:
Andrew Lang edited this companion to his fairy books, gathering true stories of adventure, escape, and war for young readers. Its contents open with A Boy among the Red Indians, told by John Tanner, and Casanova's escape, with adventures on the Findhorn and the story of Grace Darling.

Later come the Shannon and the Chesapeake, the Spartan three hundred, Prince Charlie's wanderings, and the tale of Isandhlwana and Rorke's Drift. Leif the Lucky finding Vineland the Good, the escapes of Cervantes, and Baron Trenck follow. The conquest of Montezuma's empire closes the book, with plates of Montezuma greeting the Spaniards and Cortés in the temple of Huitzilopochtli.
27603-the-red-true-story-book:
Andrew Lang's Red True Story Book gathers true stories, not fairy tales, for young readers. Its contents open with Wilson's Last Fight and The Life and Death of Joan the Maid, and run through the Bass held for King James and the crowning of Ines de Castro.

Later stories include Gustavus Vasa winning his kingdom, Sir Richard Grenville, Molly Pitcher, and the voyages of Captain Richard Falconer. Marbot's march, the wreck of the Wager, the Pitcairn Islanders, and Prince Charlie's war follow. The Burke and Wills exploring expedition and the conquest of Peru close the set. Illustrations show Joan at Chinon, the coronation of Charles VII, and King Olaf leaping overboard.
27638-the-2001-cia-world-factbook:
The CIA World Factbook 2001 gives country-by-country reference data, with information generally as of 1 January 2001, though selected data and maps were updated periodically. Its contents run from countries and locations and field listings to appendixes, notes and definitions, and a history of the Factbook.

The country listing runs alphabetically from Afghanistan, Albania, and Algeria through American Samoa, Andorra, and Angola, and onward through the Bahamas, Bahrain, and Bangladesh. Cambodia, Cameroon, and Canada follow, with the Central African Republic, Chad, and Chile, and the two Congos, the Democratic Republic and the Republic. A transcriber's note tells readers to prefix a country name with an at-sign to search it.
27675-the-1996-cia-world-factbook:
The 1996 edition of the CIA World Factbook gives country-by-country reference entries, running alphabetically from Afghanistan, Albania, and Algeria through American Samoa, Andorra, and Angola. It goes onward through the Bahamas, Bahrain, and Bangladesh to Gabon, the Gambia, and Georgia.

Each entry covers a country or territory, with its geography, people, government, and economy in the Factbook's standard form. A transcriber's note warns that the supplementary sections of this edition, such as appendixes, notes and definitions, and history, were no longer available when the file was prepared in December 2008. Readers should consult the 1995 and 1997 editions for those sections.
27676-the-1999-cia-world-factbook:
Prepared by the Central Intelligence Agency, the 1999 edition of The World Factbook gives country-by-country facts as of January 1, 1999, drawn from United States government sources. It covers geography, people, government, economy, communications, transportation, and military strength.

Entries run from Afghanistan to Zimbabwe, with oceans, disputed territories, and island dependencies included. Long a standard desk reference for officials, journalists, and students, the Factbook offers a snapshot of the world at the end of the twentieth century in compact, uniform form. Each entry follows the same order of topics, so readers can compare countries quickly.
27826-the-olive-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang edited The Olive Fairy Book, published in 1907 by Longmans, Green, and Company with eight colored plates and illustrations by H. J. Ford. It belongs to Lang's famous colored fairy-book series, following the blue, red, green, grey, yellow, pink, violet, crimson, orange, and brown volumes.

Contents include Madschun, The Blue Parrot, Geirlaug the King's Daughter, The Story of Little King Loc, and Samba the Coward, drawn from many lands. Lang's collections shaped how English children met world folklore, and the olive volume keeps the series' mix of wonder, humor, and moral luck.
27916-gabriel-and-the-hour-book:
Evaleen Stein wrote Gabriel and the Hour Book, illustrated in colors by Adelaide Everhart and published in Boston by L. C. Page and Company in July 1906, in the Roses of St. Elizabeth series. The story is set many hundred years ago in Normandy, where violets and cuckoo-buds peep through young grass.

Chapters follow Gabriel, a little color grinder, Brother Stephen's inspiration, an interview with the abbot, the hour book itself, the count's tax, and the king's illuminator. The book introduces children to medieval manuscript art through a gentle tale of craft, prayer, and Christmas.
28096-the-lilac-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang edited The Lilac Fairy Book as one volume in his long colour fairy-book series for children. The tales come from many lands, retold in clear, short prose for reading aloud. Earlier volumes in the series ran from blue and red to brown, olive, and orange, each with many pictures.

Inside are stories of clever youngest sons, enchanted beasts, cruel kings, and kind helpers who set wrongs right. Magic often turns on a promise kept or broken, and brave, polite conduct wins out over brute force. The book works well as a first shelf of world folk tales for young readers.
28314-the-yellow-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang edited The Yellow Fairy Book as one volume in his colour fairy-book series for children. The book lists Lang's other works, from Cock Lane and Common Sense to the Blue, Red, and Green Fairy Books, with plates and pictures by H. J. Ford and others. Lang retells tales from many lands in clear, short prose for reading aloud.

Stories of clever heroes, enchanted beasts, cruel kings, and kind helpers fill the volume, with magic turning on promises kept or broken. Brave, polite conduct wins out over brute force. The book works well as a shelf of world folk tales for young readers, beside its blue, red, and green companions.
28557-the-panjandrum-picture-book:
Randolph Caldecott's Panjandrum Picture Book gathers nursery rhymes with his lively illustrations, published by Frederick Warne in London and New York. The contents run from Come Lasses and Lads through Ride a Cock-Horse to Banbury Cross and A Farmer Went Trotting Upon His Grey Mare to Mrs. Mary Blaize and the Great Panjandrum himself.

Lasses and lads dance round the May-pole, with Willy and Jill, Johnny and Jone, fiddlers, and kisses, until the fiddler is paid twopence each and all go home. The Banbury Cross lady rides a white horse with rings on her fingers and bells on her toes. Caldecott's pictures make the old rhymes dance for young readers.
28716-little-mittens-for-the-little-darl:
Little Mittens for the Little Darlings, the second book of its series by the author of the Six Nightcap Books, was published by D. Appleton and Company in 1863. Fanny Barrow entered the book in 1862 and dedicated these mitten stories to Annie Louisa, her new little friend. Mr. Appleton himself, the preface jokes, demands stories for rainy days when dolls, tops, and kittens tire.

Aunt Fanny opens with a letter addressed You darling kittens, and the children feel their cheeks for whiskers. Pet insists she is a little girl, not a kitty, and the family mews in play. Contents add the Fourth Commandment, Little Sallie's long words, a little new friend, and Ilken Annie. Young readers get short tales for reading aloud.
28812-every-girl-s-book:
George F. Butler, a doctor, wrote this 1912 book for girls from ten to fourteen, the second in his How to Live series. The publisher notes that the first volume was Every Boy's Book, and that fathers and mothers should read both, so they can answer children's questions about the great facts of sex. The chapters begin with Elsie asleep in the woods, and move through bees, the husbands and wives of plants, and the first life on earth.

Later chapters explain where baby animals come from and where baby girls come from, using plants and nature as a gentle path into the subject. Butler writes plainly and kindly, aiming to replace fear and ignorance with honest knowledge. Readers get a period landmark in sex education for children, earnest, careful, and written for family reading.
29233-the-2008-cia-world-factbook:
The Central Intelligence Agency published this 2008 edition of The World Factbook, a vast reference work covering independent states, dependencies, areas of special sovereignty, and other entities. Country information was updated as of December 18, 2008. Each entry gives fields on people, government, economy, geography, communications, transportation, and military matters, with rank orders, appendixes, and notes on definitions.

New fields in this edition track education through school life expectancy and education spending as a share of gross domestic product. Five new economy fields, including the central bank discount rate, help readers grasp the global financial crisis then unfolding. Readers get a snapshot of the whole world in 2008, in the compact, field-by-field style that made the Factbook a standard reference.
29593-red-white-blue-socks-part-first-be:
Written by Aunt Fanny's Daughter, author of The Little White Angel. Aunt Fanny herself wrote an introductory chapter. Red, White, and Blue Socks was printed in New York in 1863 by Leavitt and Allen. It is part first, the first book of the Sock Stories series. Its contents open with the story of the socks, and a picture cries, Colonel, take your colors!

Helen, idly playing with a kitten in her lap, sighs that she is so tired, and wonders why rain should fall on a Friday afternoon. The tales that follow are gentle, patriotic, and domestic, made for children of the Civil War years. Young readers and students of children's books will find a sweet, period volume of stories stitched with red, white, and blue.
29595-funny-little-socks-being-the-fourt:
Funny Little Socks, the fourth book of the Sock Stories by Aunt Fanny's Daughter, was printed in New York in 1863 by Leavitt and Allen. It is dedicated to darling little Allie Baby, and its contents open with Little Mother, Dolls at Housekeeping, and The Fairy Wish. A picture shows the children giving Gawow a dance, in the book's playful spirit.

Kitty, praised as her mamma's little mother for the day, loves her mother and wants to save her all the trouble she can. The tales that follow are gentle lessons in kindness, play, and home life for young children. Readers of Victorian children's books will find a charming, small volume of domestic fancy from the Civil War years.
29635-dr-montessori-s-own-handbook:
Maria Montessori, author of The Montessori Method and Pedagogical Anthropology, wrote Dr. Montessori's Own Handbook, printed in 1914 by Frederick A. Stokes Company of New York, with forty-three pictures. Its contents run from a preface and introductory remarks through a children's house and the method, to didactic material for the education of the senses. The book is dedicated to Donna Maria Maraini, who upheld the work with sacrifice.

Montessori sets out her method in her own words: prepared surroundings, sense training, and respect for the child's self-direction. The handbook serves teachers and parents who would try the method at home or school. Students of education will find a primary source from the founder herself.
29939-the-chinese-fairy-book:
Dr. R. Wilhelm edited The Chinese Fairy Book, translated after original sources by Frederick H. Martens and printed in New York in 1921 by Frederick A. Stokes Company. George W. Hood drew six pictures in color for the book. It belongs to a Fairy Series that also holds English, Welsh, Irish, Scottish, Italian, Hungarian, Indian, Jewish, and Swedish volumes.

Nursery fairy tales open the contents: Women's Words Part Flesh and Blood, The Three Rhymsters, and How Greed for a Trifling Thing Led a Man to Lose a Great One. The Magic Cask, The Bird with Nine Heads, The Great Flood, and The Fox and the Tiger follow, with Why Dog and Cat Are Enemies. Legends of the gods follow, from How the Five Ancients Became Men to the herd boy and the weaving maiden, Yang Oerlang, and Notscha.
31102-stevenson-memorial-cook-book:
Compiled by Mrs William D. Hurlbut and published in Chicago in 1919, this cook book served the Sarah Hackett Stevenson Memorial Lodging House Association, to whose namesake it is dedicated. Its index runs from appetizers and soups through meats, fish, vegetables, breads, cakes, pies, and candies, with sections on preserves, salads, sauces, and household hints as well.

A foreword recalls unemployed women on Chicago streets in 1893, the need that first called the lodging house into being, and the service work behind the volume. Beyond its recipes, the book preserves the everyday cooking of its time and the charitable project that gathered them, making it useful both in the kitchen and as social history.
31201-the-brown-fairy-book:
Edited by Andrew Lang and published by Longmans, Green in 1904, with illustrations by H. J. Ford, The Brown Fairy Book gathers tales from around the world. Its preface notes stories told by Native North American grandmothers, tales from Aboriginal children in the Australian bush, and a sacred-milk tale from southern Africa. It also notes Pivi and Kabo from New Caledonia, where a boy might not speak to his own sisters.

Dedicated to Diana Scott Lang, the volume sits in Lang's famous colored fairy-book series, mixing wonder, manners, and morals for young readers. The collection's range, from ball-carriers and bunyips to island customs, makes it a lasting sampler of the world's storytelling.
32202-the-irish-fairy-book:
Alfred Perceval Graves's The Irish Fairy Book, illustrated by George Denham and published in London by T. Fisher Unwin, is an anthology of Irish fairy tales, songs, and lore. It opens with A Faery Song, sung by faery folk over Diarmuid and Grania, asleep in bridal sleep beneath a cromlech. The singers call themselves old, old and gay, thousands of years old if all were told. They give the children silence and love, the long dew-dropping hours of night, and the stars above.

Its contributors include Standish James O'Grady, Patrick Kennedy, William Allingham, T. Crofton Croker, W. B. Yeats, Juliana Horatia Ewing, Sir Samuel Ferguson, Patrick Weston Joyce, William Carleton, Samuel Lover, Jeremiah Curtin, Lady Wilde, Sheridan Le Fanu, Douglas Hyde, and Dora Sigerson. Readers get a wide Irish fairy anthology, from folk collectors to poets, gathered under one cover with illustrations.
32210-the-brownies-their-book:
Palmer Cox's The Brownies: Their Book, published in New York by Appleton-Century-Crofts with copyright in 1887 and renewed in 1915, is a children's picture book of sprites. Its caption explains that Brownies, like fairies and goblins, are imaginary little sprites fond of harmless pranks and helpful deeds. They frolic and labour while weary homes rest, and stay unseen by any human gaze.

Its contents include The Brownies at School, The Brownies' Ride, and The Brownies on Skates, with illustrations throughout and a presentation page reading This book belongs to, and Presented by. Readers get Cox's classic Brownie book, where tiny helpers prank and aid by night, unseen. The verse and pictures made the Brownies a nursery favourite, and this edition preserves the original charm.
32321-the-book:
Michael Shaara's short story, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in November 1953, follows a young officer to a world cut off from the universe. Its tagline describes a world, cut off from the universe, that had universal wisdom, and facing death at every moment, that had the secret of peace. Beauclaire is given his first ship at Sirius. Called before the Commandant in the afternoon heat, he shuffles awkwardly, delighted, on the shaggy carpet.

Beauclaire, aged twenty-five and fresh from the Academy by two months, faces a splendid day. The Commandant, an old man with a face of many lines, is old, hot, tired, and very irritated. At his age, talking to a young man irritates, because the young are bright, certain, and knowing nothing. Readers get a space story of youth and age.
32836-when-the-mountain-shook:
Robert Abernathy sends two fugitive lovers toward a black geometric mountain, in a story from IF Worlds of Science Fiction of March 1954. Var and Neena flee a feud between their peoples, sealed by love at the Truce of New Grass. If her father and kinsmen overtake them, Var faces death and Neena living shame.

Var spins a dream onto the pass behind them: lurid fire from the Ryzga mountain, strange lights, an avalanche, and beasts rushing from crevices. The dream will not hold pursuers long, so the pair press on over glare ice and bottomless crevices toward the Watcher's cave. The Watcher teaches them the mountain's structure and its guardian machines. Inside Ryzga itself, they must choose between a sacrifice of shame and a separation they cannot bear.
33047-the-eye-of-wilbur-mook:
H. B. Hickey's story, from Amazing Stories in November 1948, follows Wilbur Mook, a young man woken by his mother's call that he will be late for work. He rises slowly from a beautiful dream in which he had Peter Bellows down and was punching his head. He opens one eye to a clock showing eight o'clock and flings off his covers. The dream's triumph and the morning's rush set the story's comic contrast.

An illustration shows a cloud of smoke, a horrid visage, and Mook's legs growing weak beneath him, hinting at the strange eye of the title and the trouble it brings. Hickey keeps the tale light and pulp-quick, letting an ordinary working morning slide into something uncanny. It is a short, amusing story about a daydreamer whose dreams, and eyes, prove harder to control than he expects.
33246-civic-league-cook-book:
The Civic League Cook Book gathers recipes and household hints from Williston, North Dakota, framed by local ads for flour, groceries, farm loans, and drug stores. Its pages mix practical cookery with the life of a small prairie town, where merchants, banks, and hotels all had a stake in the league's work. The recipes favor plain, hearty food made from home-grown wheat and pantry staples, suited to farm kitchens.

Beyond its dishes, the book is a snapshot of community life in the early twentieth century, when a civic league could rally a town around a shared table. Readers who cook will find usable old recipes; readers of local history will find names, firms, and daily needs preserved in print. It is a modest volume, but a rich one for those who prize place and past.
33502-my-knitting-book:
Miss Lambert, author of the Hand-book of Needlework, published this practical knitting manual in London in 1843 at eighteen pence. The preface explains that its examples were chosen with care, many of them original, and arranged so that even a novice can follow them. Large, distinct type was adopted because knitting was a favored evening amusement of older readers and invalids.

The contents run from explanations of knitting terms and the standard filière through cuffs, muffatees, caps, comforters, lace, insertions, muffs, waistcoat stitches, and twelve patterns for doyleys and tidies. Some examples repeat material from her earlier handbook, but most are new. The book remains a charming record of Victorian domestic craft and a usable pattern source.
33547-the-grey-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang's Grey Fairy Book, edited by Lang with illustrations by H. J. Ford, gathers fairy tales from many lands. Published in New York and London in 1905, with copyright in 1900, the book's frontispiece shows a dervish drowning pigs, and its goblin pony hints at the wonders within. Lang, famed for his colored fairy books, chose tales to delight children and adults alike.

The volume's charm lies in its varied, well-told tales, from far countries and old traditions, with Ford's pictures to guide the eye. Its tone is timeless and gentle, suited to reading aloud. For lovers of fairy lore, The Grey Fairy Book offers a handsome, classic collection, grey in name but bright in wonder.
33571-the-green-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang edited this collection of fairy tales drawn from many countries, presenting it as the third of his color fairy books after the Blue and Red volumes. The tales come from France, Germany, Russia, Italy, Scotland, England, and China, among other sources, and the edition carries numerous illustrations by H. J. Ford. Lang addresses young readers directly in his preface, explaining that children asked for more stories after each earlier book.

The volume offers enchanted quests, clever youngest children, talking creatures, and villains undone by their own pride, in the plain storytelling style of the series. Its range makes it useful both as bedtime reading and as a survey of how similar tale patterns appear across cultures. Families looking for classic fairy tales will find a generous and varied selection here.
33951-the-ladies-knitting-and-netting-bo:
Miss Watts wrote this second series of knitting and netting lessons, published in London in 1840 in a second edition. It gives patterns for gentlemen's gloves, mittens, cuffs, muffatees, and peacock stitch work, then turns to cushion covers, sofa pillows, table mats, napkin rings, and purses. Each lesson is short and practical.
