Watts writes for ladies who already hold needle and thread, and her directions assume a working knowledge of the craft. The book preserves the home needlework of its age in exact detail. It still serves makers who like period patterns and plain, step-by-step instruction.
34423-jack-and-the-check-book:
John Kendrick Bangs, a famed American humorist, wrote Jack and the Check Book for Harper and Brothers in 1911, with art by Albert Levering. The tale starts like Jack and the Beanstalk retold for the age of banks. A poor widow has lost her savings in mining shares and faces bills she cannot pay, and her son Jack must find a way out.

Six long parts follow a magic check book, a Great Wish Syndicate, Puss the promoter, a golden fleece, an unseen cloak, and the return of Aladdin. Bangs uses fairy tale goods to mock Wall Street deals, quick wealth schemes, and high finance talk. The fun stays light but the point is sharp.
34470-the-blue-jar-story-book:
Blue Jar Story Book is a set of tales for children by several hands. Maria Edgeworth, Charles Lamb, Mary Lamb, and Alicia Mant lead the named authors. McLoughlin Brothers of New York issued the pictured book in nineteen o six. Contents list six tales, opening with The Blue Jar itself.

Edgeworth tale begins with Rosamond, a girl of about seven, in London. She walks with her mother past shop windows full of strange goods. She does not know the use or names of half the things she sees. Crowds, carts, and barrows make her cling to her mother hand tight. At a toy shop she cries how happy she would be there. Moral tales of wishes and conduct fill the small volume for young readers.
3454-the-lilac-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang edits this volume of fairy tales, one of his famous colored fairy books for children. In his preface he answers the dinner party question he hears most often, whether he is writing another fairy book. He answers with the same patience he gives to lawyers, dentists, and clergymen asked about their work. The tales that follow come from many lands and many storytellers.

Inside are princes and witches, clever youngest children, enchanted animals, and quests that reward kindness and courage. Lang keeps the stories short and plain, so they read well aloud at bedtime. The book suits families who want classic tales in their old form, without modern retelling or moral lectures tacked on.
34822-the-century-cook-book:
Mary Ronald put together The Century Cook Book, held by the Century firm from 1895 and printed in a 1901 New York form. The book gives steps for cooking in all its branches, from plain home dishes to high class and fancy show pieces. A group of New England dishes came from Susan Coolidge, and some Southern dishes are added.

Beyond recipes, Ronald teaches how to serve dinners, dress the table, and run the social side of meals at home. A quote from Ruskin at the front praises the good cook for care, thrift, taste, and much tasting with no waste. French sayings on food and drink open the work with wit.
35027-mr-punch-s-railway-book:
Punch's Railway Book is a book of jest from the great jest sheet of London. Hammerton saw the set through the press. It stands in the same set of jest books as its sea side mate. One mint and sixty plates stand in this book. The draw men of those plates are named on the title leaf. May, du Maurier, and Keene stand first in that roll.

Leech, Tenniel, Reed, Ravenhill, Partridge, and Cleaver stand past them in that roll. More gay art hands than those are named there as well. The set list at the front names five and twenty books of the set. Life in the great town, life in the wilds, and life in the high lands stand in it. Jest of the Scots, of the Irish, and of the town poor fill the roll.
35458-the-green-forest-fairy-book:
The Green Forest Fairy Book, by Loretta Ellen Brady, was printed in Boston by Little, Brown, and Company under a 1920 copyright. Alice B Preston drew the plates. Brady gives the book to the boys and girls of Little Jim Wards at the San Francisco Childrens Hospital, .

A prologue opens the tales, then Dame Grumble and Her Curious Apple Tree. A Tale of the Northland Kingdom and The Little Tree That Never Grew Up follow. The Tale of Punchinello, The Strange Tale of the Brown Bear, and The Beggar Princess fill the mid part. Sweep and Little Sweep, The Goose Girl and the Blue Gander, and a tale for Halloween close the set. The prologue tells that long ago, when the world was young, fairy folk still lived in the greenwoods. Young readers get new fairy tales.
35506-cloud-city-cook-book:
The Cloud City Cook Book, by Mrs William H Nash, was printed at Leadville, Colorado, in 1889 for cooks working a mile and more above the sea. Leadville's nickname gives the book its name.

The preface explains why a mining town needed its own cook book. At high altitude, the ladies of the Congregational Church argue, cooking follows its own laws. Amounts of ingredients, cooking times, and even fuel needs differ from the lowlands, because water boils at a lower heat. New wives from the East must learn the new rules before their dinners match those of home. The recipes that follow come from local kitchens, each signed by its contributor, and cover the full range of family meals.
35829-the-2009-cia-world-factbook:
The 2009 CIA World Factbook is the Central Intelligence Agency's annual reference of country profiles, here in its 2009 state with updates logged through the thirteenth of November that year. The book opens with a guide to country profiles, then gives its contents by section: countries and locations, field listings, rank orders, and appendixes.

Each profile gathers a country's geography, people, government, economy, communications, transportation, and military into set fields. The update log at the front records elections and changes of government from Afghanistan to Uruguay, twenty revised economy fields, and new space and ground photographs. Rank orders let a reader compare countries field by field across the whole world. The Factbook began as a classified aid and became the standard one-volume survey of every land on earth.
35830-the-2010-cia-world-factbook:
The CIA World Factbook for 2010 gathers standard profiles of the countries and locations of the world, with a guide to country profiles, field listings, rank orders, appendixes, and notes and definitions. A history of the Factbook and a frequently asked questions section round out the front matter.

A What's New log at the front records the site's weekly updates into January 2011. It lists new space-based photographs for Australia, China, Namibia, Mexico, and the United States, and the whole economy category refreshed for 2010 and earlier years. New fields cover national anthems and volcanism under natural hazards. Trivia prompts point readers into the book. They ask which country's flag is only one color, what airport handles the most passengers, and where the Netherlands reaches its highest elevation, which is not in Europe.
35991-domesday-book:
Edgar Lee Masters writes a long poem in Domesday Book, printed in London in 1921. Eveleigh Nash issue the book, with copyright in the United States held by Macmillan. Masters had writ Spoon River Anthology. He gives this book to his father, Hardin Wallace Masters, in a dedication cut short in praise.

The front pages are crowded with press opinions of the earlier book. One of the greatest books of the present century, says the Nation of Spoon River. A London chronicle praises its originality of conception and treatment, and a daring that would soar to the stars. Edward Garnett, in a Manchester paper, holds that Masters will become a classic. Its language is outspoken, he notes, destructive of cant and pharisaism, and piercingly true in insight. The new volume asks to be read in that light.
35997-the-jungle-book:
Rudyard Kipling's Jungle Book, copyrighted in 1893 and 1894, is printed here by the Century Company in 1910. Seven tales stand in the contents, each followed by a song. Mowgli's Brothers opens the book; Kaa's Hunting and Tiger Tiger continue the wolf child's story. The White Seal leaves India for the northern seas, and Rikki-Tikki-Tavi fights the cobras in an English bungalow garden. Toomai of the Elephants and Her Majesty's Servants close the volume.

The songs belong to the tales they follow: the Hunting-Song of the Seeonee Pack, the Road-Song of the Bandar-log, Darzee's Chaunt, and the Parade-Song of the Camp Animals. A long list of illustrations names the plates, from the tiger's roar in the cave to Little Toomai looking down on scores of broad backs. The frontispiece shows Toomai laid along Kala Nag's great neck.
36008-the-blue-rose-fairy-book:
The Blue Rose Fairy Book is a book of fairy tales by Maurice Baring, published by Dodd, Mead and Company at New York in 1911. Baring dedicated it to Mary and Aubrey. A note says one tale, The Glass Mender, first appeared in the English Review, and six shorter tales in the Morning Post; the rest are new. The front picture shows a rider whose horse's hoofs leave a trail of anemones behind.

Twelve tales fill the book, starting with The Glass Mender and the title tale of the blue rose. The Story of Vox Angelica and Lieblich Gedacht follows, a tale of a boy who climbs into the heart of an organ. The Vagabond, The Minstrel, The Silver Mountain, and Orestes and the Dragon stand among the rest, closing with The Wise Princess.
36026-from-pillar-to-post-leaves-from-a-:
John Kendrick Bangs, the humorist who wrote The House-Boat on the Styx, set down leaves from a lecturer's note-book in From Pillar to Post. The Century Company issued the book at New York in 1916, with pictures by Jno R Neill. Bangs looks back on ten years of platform work, speaking in halls across America and Canada. His note at the front thanks the Lyceum bureaus for loyal work.

He jokes that their zeal once booked him in Winnipeg on Monday night and New Orleans on Tuesday, with side trips to San Diego and Maine close behind. He counts the mad pace a tribute to his speed rather than a wrong. The chapters give a warm, funny view of the lecture circuit of his day, when a known writer earned much of his bread by talking to town audiences.
3672-the-2000-cia-world-factbook:
This volume reproduces the Central Intelligence Agency's World Factbook for the year 2000, as prepared for Project Gutenberg by Martin Pedersen from the agency's online edition. It gives short profiles of every country and territory, from Egypt and El Salvador to Fiji, Finland, France, and French Guiana, with facts on geography, people, government, economy, and communications.

Readers should note that the Gutenberg edition omits the original maps and graphics, and that tables may not align perfectly after conversion. The Factbook itself is a reference snapshot, not a narrative, and later editions replaced it online. The volume suits researchers who want a compact, year 2000 picture of the world as American officials summarized it.
36755-the-child-s-picture-book:
The Child's Picture Book is a small illustrated primer printed at Concord, New Hampshire, by Rufus Merrill in 1849. Merrill was a bookseller as well as publisher. The book opens with the alphabet in capitals and small letters, then the numbers one to nought.

Each page pairs a woodcut with a few plain words. The Good Samaritan tends the man who fell among thieves. A steam ship sails to all parts of the world, and a steam boat follows. The cow gives milk, lambs frolic in the fields, and boys spin a top. A duck, a pitcher, a bell, a chair, and a horse fill out the set. The whole is built for a child who is still joining letters to things, with Bible and farm and machine side by side.
37193-the-swedish-fairy-book:
The Swedish Fairy Book, edited by Clara Stroebe, brings Swedish tales into English. Martens made the translation, and Hood painted eight plates in colour. Stokes held the copyright of 1921 in New York, where the book was printed.

A frontispiece catches the magic mid-stroke: no sooner had he spoken than he lay in a splendid room. Twenty-eight tales follow, of giants and trolls. Finn the giant and the minster of Lund stand early, with the Skalunda giant. Yuletide specters, a werewolf, and a girl with a snake keep the dark strain. Silverwhite draws his sword on a sea-troll in one plate. A pike rises with golden keys in his mouth. Charcoal Nils meets a troll-woman, and three dogs and a poor devil close the run.
37303-the-girls-of-central-high-on-the-s:
Gertrude W Morrison wrote The Girls of Central High on the Stage, or The Play That Took the Prize, held in 1914. Morrison had writ past books in the same series, set at Central High and at Lake Luna. Twenty five chapters carry the school tale. Jess Morse stands at its heart.

Chapter heads are built on the word needed, again and again. What the M O R group needed leads the tale. What Jess, Mr Chumley, and Mrs Prentice needed come next. A skating party, mid term tests, and a ski run fill the middle. Dress trials, a great night, and good news for Jess close the plot. A front print shows Jess step forth, shy, to face the crowd.
37348-the-old-fashioned-fairy-book:
The Old-Fashioned Fairy Book was written by Mrs Harrison. Sampson Low published it in London. Emmet drew the illustrations. Harrison gives the tales to Fairfax, Frank, and Archy. Seventeen fairy stories fill the first part. The Princess Eglantine leads them. Dame Martha's step-daughter meets the grandmother of the gnomes. A magic coffee-mill serves Annette; a little white mouse serves Juliet. The Ice King's bride and a turkey-queen have tales of their own. A leperhaun closes the fairy part. Romances of the Middle Ages form a second part. Sir Isumbras is tried there, and Bisclaveret runs as a wolf.

Roswal and Lilian, Eliduc, and a falcon-king follow. A poem, Fairy Days, opens the volume in verse. A nurse's knee and a hall fire frame its memories.
37364-the-second-jungle-book:
The Second Jungle Book, by Rudyard Kipling with decorations by his father, John Lockwood Kipling, was copyrighted in 1895 and issued in New York by the Century company. A verse motto heads the contents: the head and the hoof of the Law and the haunch and the hump is, obey. Tales and songs alternate through the book, as in the first Jungle Book.

How Fear Came opens the set, then The Law of the Jungle in verse. The Miracle of Purun Bhagat leaves the jungle for the hills. Letting in the Jungle, The King's Ankus, Quiquern, Red Dog, and The Spring Running carry Mowgli's story on. Songs of Kabir, the little hunter, and Chil the kite fall between the tales. Kipling deepens the first book's world: law, fear, and the slow parting of boy and pack.
37532-the-scottish-fairy-book:
The Scottish Fairy Book, by Elizabeth Grierson, with illustrations by Meredith Williams, was printed by Lippincott at Philadelphia. It belongs to a Fairy Series with English, Welsh, Irish, Italian, and other national volumes. A motto from Gavin Douglas heads it: of brownies and of bogles full this book.

Some thirty tales fill the contents. Thomas the Rhymer opens the collection. Thomas Learmont, laird of Ercildoune in Berwickshire, a young gallant fond of books, poetry, and music, wanders one sunny May morning into the woods by the Huntly Burn. Gold Tree and Silver Tree, Whippety Stourie, and The Red Etin follow. Sea and beast tales include The Seal Catcher and the Merman and The Black Bull of Norroway. Later pieces offer The Wee Bannock, Habetrot the spinstress, Assipattle and the Mester Stoorworm, Katherine Crackernuts, and The Well of the World's End.
37680-the-myrtle-reed-cook-book:
Myrtle Reed wrote The Myrtle Reed Cook Book, put out by Putnam of New York. Rights were held from 1905, 1906, and 1911, and the Knickerbocker Press made this form in 1916. The front pages boast a million copies sold of Reed works. An opening note says the firm knows of no other book quite like this one. The contents start with a part on the thought and art of breakfast. How to set the table and a set of kitchen verses come next.

From there the book works through fruits, cereals, salt fish, and more day by day foods. Reed was known for tales and gift books, not just for the stove. Here her bright voice turns to the home table and the craft of meals. Cooks got both sound steps and charm in one book.
37740-the-civil-war-centennial-handbook:
The Civil War Centennial Handbook is a fact guide by William Price. The book was made for the full age mark of the war of the states. Parts split the tale into facts, prints, dress, dates, and relic lore. The book came out in the year nineteen sixty one.

Heads call that war the first of the modern kind in its tools and scale. Prints show camp life, spies, faith at the front, and air scouts in turn. Dress plates sort blue and grey garb by rank and by home state. A date list of fights and a map close the small keen guide. The book served the crowds who thronged fields at the cent mark year.
37995-the-diamond-fairy-book:
Hutchinson and Company gather fairy tales from many lands in a gilt gift book issued at Paternoster Row, London. Eight coloured plates by Frank Papé and eighty-two drawings by H R Millar fill it. The price was three shillings and sixpence.

The series stands uniform with its sisters. The Ruby, Golden, and Silver Fairy Books share the shelf and the artists. Twelve writers sign this volume's tales. Isabel Bellerby and Mrs Egerton Eastwick write in English. Z Topelius brings Finland, and Clemens Brentano and W Hauff bring Germany. Xavier Marmier and Saint-Juirs bring France. The opening tale tells of four kings: North of perpetual snow, South of year-round sun, East of the cold winds, and West of the gentle zephyrs. Princess Crystal leads the contents.
38046-business-english-a-practice-book:
Business English: A Practice Book, by Rose Buhlig of Tilden High School, Chicago, was published in Boston, New York, and Chicago in 1914. The book trains students in the English they need for office work. A note from Columbia University dated January 1914 fronts the text.

Part one covers word study, pronunciation, spelling rules, and grammar, from nouns to verbs and joining words. Part two turns to speech and writing: clear sentences, paragraphs, punctuation, and business letters. Part three applies the skills to trade topics such as making and shipping goods. Drills and practice tasks fill the book, aimed at teens who would soon write letters, bills, and reports for pay.
38070-the-norwegian-fairy-book:
The Norwegian Fairy Book is a collection of Norwegian folk tales. Clara Stroebe edited it, and Martens translated the tales. Stokes published it in New York, with a 1922 copyright. Six colour illustrations by George Hood accompany the text. It belongs to a Fairy Series of many nations' tales. English, Welsh, Irish, Scottish, and Italian volumes are listed. Per Gynt opens the contents of this Norwegian volume. The Isle of Udrost and The Three Lemons follow.

The Neighbour Underground and The Secret Church come next. The Comrade and Aspenclog give longer tales in the list. An illustration shows an old woman limping up to a traveller. She asks him what he has in his knapsack, the caption says. The tales come from Norway's oral tradition of trolls and heroes. Stroebe's series carried folk tales to American children.
38193-new-royal-cook-book:
The New Royal Cook Book is a home cook guide from the Royal Baking Powder firm. Its right claim bears the year nineteen twenty from that firm. Plain steps for sound and tasty home fare fill its pages, the front says. Young house wives get full clear guides to cakes and sweet goods. Skilled cooks find old picks plus hints to save eggs and dear goods.

Each dish in the book was tried out many times, the front claims. Royal powder is the rise agent in each dish that needs one. Sour milk and soda swaps are warned off as a cause of flops. Its name list runs from salt nuts and angel cake to bean soup. Breads, pies, drinks, and canned fruit stand in that long list.
38215-the-mary-frances-cook-book:
The Mary Frances Cook Book teaches cooking to girls through a story. Jane Eayre Fryer wrote the book. She copyrighted it in 1912. Its subtitle promises adventures among the kitchen people. Margaret Hays drew the full-page pictures. The dedication speaks to all girls who love to help mother.

An opening letter explains the device. Mary Frances longs to help her mother. The kitchen tools come alive as her teachers. Aunty Rolling Pin leads the cast. Toaster Man and others join her. Chapters mix tales with real recipes. One treats jacket-boiled potatoes. Another stages a pot-and-kettle fight. The girl gives a cooking lesson before the book ends. She comes out a real little woman.
39278-the-portland-sketch-book:
The Portland Sketch Book, edited by Ann Stephens, was printed at Portland, Maine, in 1836. Its aim was to gather work by Portland writers in one small volume. Only those born in the city or long resident there were admitted. The preface marvels at the list for a town of hardly fifteen thousand souls. Henry Wadsworth Longfellow stands among the names, with John Neal and Nathaniel Parker Willis.

The editor sought fresh pieces from living authors. She met delays and broken promises, she admits. Dead writers are drawn from their printed works. A piece on descriptions of the divine being is noted for its Hebrew text. The book is a civic showcase, made to prove that a small port town could hold its own in letters.
39891-jewel-mysteries-from-a-dealer-s-no:
Max Pemberton's Jewel Mysteries, from a dealer's note book, was published in New York in 1904 by Fenno and Company. Pemberton had written The Iron Pirate and Kronstadt before it. Ten tales make the book, each named for a stone or a jewel: an opal, green diamonds, emeralds, a topaz, rubies, and sapphires.

The first tale opens on a wet, dark day in Piccadilly, with the dealer alone in his shop after six hours without a customer. As he reaches to shut the great safe, the mirror shows a strange man at the counter, in a long black coat smothered in astrachan that no English tailor made. Into the dealer's hand goes the opal of Carmalovitch, and the note book begins.
40943-miss-leslie-s-new-cookery-book:
Miss Leslie's New Cookery Book was published at Philadelphia. Peterson issued the volume from Chestnut Street. Its own advertisement fronts this copy in full. The book runs to 652 pages, bound, the notice says. Hundreds of receipts fill it, all of them new. Soups, fish, oysters, and every meat are covered in turn. Terrapins, turtle, vegetables, and sauces follow. Bread, pickles, sweetmeats, and cakes of both kinds are treated. Preparations for the sick have their own section. Lists tell what dishes suit each season together. Breakfasts, dinners, and suppers are planned for large and small families. Every receipt was tried by the author herself, the notice swears.

None stands in any of her former books. Newspaper praise is quoted at length behind the notice. No cook book in the world, the publisher claims, is more complete.
42134-the-violet-book:
The Violet Book holds verse and prose on one small flower, picked by Willis Allen. Verse heads claim the violet is the poets own flower past all save the rose. A gift page names the girl for whom the set was first made. Rights date the work to the year nineteen nine.

Old Greek song and Roman verse both lend the bloom a place of praise. Great prose men of Rome held the flower dear, the talk notes with care. Lines from Browning on a May morn of violets head the title page. Songs, tales, and lore bits form a small wreath round the shy bloom. The book served as a gift for fans of verse and of spring.
43327-rodin-the-man-and-his-art-with-lea:
Rodin: The Man and His Art, with leaves from his note-book, was compiled by Judith Cladel and issued by the Century Company in 1917. Star translated the French text, and James Huneker wrote the introduction. Photographs illustrate the volume throughout. Huneker opens by calling Rodin, born at Paris in 1840, the master among living sculptors. He traces the fight for bread and schooling, the failed entry to the Beaux-Arts, and the years ghosting for other sculptors in Belgium.

The Man with the Broken Nose, refused by the Salon, anchors the early story. Huneker then studies Rodin's handling of light and movement, the widened surfaces that give his figures their glow. The note-book leaves let Rodin speak in his own words on art. Cladel, who knew the sculptor, shapes the record of a career built with no steady schooling.
43879-substitutes-for-flesh-foods-vegeta:
Substitutes for Flesh Foods is a vegetarian cook book by Fulton. It was issued by the Pacific Press Publishing Company of Oakland, California, with copyright in 1904. The author's preface tells why the book was written.

Fulton argues that men and women need sound advice on food more than ever. Doctors and dentists grow in number, yet stomachs wear out and patent cures sell by the ton. Disease among cattle, poultry, and fish has grown so fast, he says, that flesh is no longer safe. The book turns instead to grains, nuts, vegetables, and fruits. Its recipes aim to give a full diet with no meat at all.
44730-memorabilia-mathematica-or-the-phi:
Memorabilia Mathematica, or the Philomath's Quotation-Book, by Robert Edouard Moritz, professor of mathematics in the University of Washington, was published by Macmillan in New York in 1914. Twenty one chapters gather quotations on the science, each passage credited to its author and source.

The chapters define the object and nature of mathematics, then take up its value, its teaching, and study and research in it. Modern mathematics and the mathematician follow. Two chapters give persons and anecdotes. Later chapters treat mathematics as a fine art and as a language. Mathematics and logic, philosophy, and science come next. Arithmetic, algebra, geometry, and the calculus close the survey. Paradoxes and curiosities end the book. Chapter one quotes Sylvester on the word mathematics, and Descartes on a general science of order and measure.
44915-margaret-brown-s-french-cookery-bo:
Margaret Brown's French cookery book, published at Washington in 1886, promises receipts from the plainest cookery to the most elaborate French dish. Its contents are arranged alphabetically, and they run for pages.

Soups open the book: asparagus, celery, consommé, and clam chowder. Chicken appears à l'Italienne, in croquettes, rissoles, pie à la Reine, and glacé. There are courses planned for a dinner of twelve, a spring lunch, and a spring breakfast. Puddings crowd the pages: cabinet, cottage, plum, and Delmonico's. Boned turkey, canvasback ducks, Charlotte Russe, and chocolate transparent icing all find places. American cooks of the Gilded Age get a working kitchen library, French in ambition, plain in much of its matter.
45968-the-art-of-the-book:
Charles Holme edited The Art of the Book, a review of recent work in Europe and America in type, page decoration, and binding, issued by The Studio in nineteen fourteen. A prefatory note thanks the Kelmscott Press for leave to copy pages in the three types designed by William Morris. Emery Walker helped with those copies and with a page of Proctor's Greek type. Pages from the Eragny, Ashendene, and Riccardi presses also appear.

The list of articles opens with British types for printing books, by Newdigate, and fine binding in England, by Cockerell. Later pieces treat the art of the book in Germany, France, Austria, Hungary, and Sweden. Binders, founders, and printers across the continent sent work to be shown. The volume is a survey of the fine press world at its height.
46108-the-playwork-book:
The Playwork Book is a craft manual for children by Ann Macbeth. McBride issued it in New York in 1918. It carries 114 diagrams. The contents list runs to more than a hundred small projects. A woolen ball and a sprig of flowers open the list. Skipping ropes, dolls, and toy furniture follow. Kites, catapults, and a model aeroplane close the range.

Each project is a thing to make from scraps. Corks, feathers, rushes, and fish bones all serve. A tea set is made from fish bones. Furniture is woven from rush and raffia. Sound toys include whistles, drums, and a telephone. The introduction speaks of the child who never grows up. That child, Macbeth says, keeps the keys of heaven. The book joins play to hand training for the home.
46341-nat-goodwin-s-book:
Nat Goodwins Book is the stage life tale of the actor Nat Goodwin, out in nineteen fourteen. A Boston house brought it out with plates through its long scheme. First parts tell his school end day and his first step on a stage. Great stage men of his age crowd the early parts as hosts. Irving, Jefferson, and McCullough stand in that first row of names.

Stage rule fights, rink turns, and play house gold days fill mid parts. Parts on Gilbert, Riley, Cohan, and Drew show his wide range of mates. A day at Reno and a fight won with a doubt mark give spice. Late parts roam to Samoa, Honolulu, and the land of the kangaroo. Thoughts born of small stage work and a last wife jest close the book.
47335-food-for-the-mind-or-a-new-riddle-:
Food for the Mind, or a New Riddle-Book, is a children's riddle book printed at London in 1778. Carnan and Newbery sold it at Saint Paul's Church Yard. The compiler hides behind a grand pen name: John-the-Giant-Killer, Esquire. The book is made for the great and the little good boys and girls of England, Scotland, and Ireland.

Its motto cries, come riddle me, riddle me, riddle me ree. Verses from Homer and Puffendorf dress the title page in mock learning. A notice warns buyers to take care: one Newbery at the corner of the churchyard has no concern in the late John Newbery's books. The introduction calls riddling the art of both dissembling and undissembling. Inside, question and answer verses offer a Georgian child's parlour game in print.
48-the-1992-cia-world-factbook:
The Central Intelligence Agency's 1992 Factbook surveys the world country by country. This edition, dated January 1, 1993, keeps the agency's standard pattern for officials. Each entry covers land, people, government, economy, and defense.

Afghanistan opens the alphabetical run, with area compared to Texas and borders listed in detail. Similar entries follow for every recognized state and territory. The 1992 volume catches new states rising from the Soviet collapse. It remains a useful snapshot of that turning year. Researchers pair this edition with the 1990 and 1991 volumes to trace the Soviet breakup. Its country notes still help readers date the new post-Soviet map.
48281-the-china-painter-instruction-book:
The China Painter Instruction Book came from Thayer and Chandler at Chicago in a second edition. Rights were held in 1914 by that house. Contents open with color mixing and color combinations in short order. A conventional style part follows, then flower, leaf, fruit, and figure painting. Tinting, ground laying, dusting, outlining, and cutting out take their turns in the list.

Pads and dabbers, slow and quick drying colors, and paste or relief work come next. Gold, gold burnishing, lustres, matt colors, and banding fill the middle. Oxidizing, glazing, chipping, enamel work, china repairing, and firing china close the book. The first lesson warns that clean tools and well mixed colors are essential. Powder color is set on a clean slab with mixing medium, to a thick paste. The palette knife, kept flat, blends it with a rotary motion till smooth.
48605-the-russian-story-book:
The Russian Story Book retells tales from the old song cycles of Kiev and Novgorod. Richard Wilson retold them, and Macmillan published the book in London in 1916. Frank C Papé supplied colored plates and line drawings.

The hero Ilya opens the book, healed after thirty years as a cripple. Stories follow Ilya against Svyatogor and Nightingale the Robber. Other tales tell of Dunai, Nikitich, and Vasily the Turbulent. These songs preserve the heroic age of early Russia. Wilson shaped them for English readers in prose. Such retellings carried folk epics to children far from their source.
49068-the-whistler-book:
Sadakichi Hartmann wrote The Whistler Book, published in Boston by Page and Company in 1910. Its subtitle calls it a monograph on the life and standing of James McNeill Whistler. Fifty-seven reproductions of Whistler's key works fill the volume. A portrait by Boldini fronts the book.

Chapters trace Whistler from the Latin Quarter and Chelsea onward. Hartmann studies his art of omission and his problems of light and tone. Symphonies in interior decoration get a chapter of their own. Later chapters cover his iconoclasm and the man as his friends knew him. A bibliography and lists of paintings and nocturnes close the volume. The book argues for Whistler's place while his fame was still contested.
49146-the-shakespeare-story-book:
Mary Macleod retells Shakespeare's plays as stories for young readers in a book issued by A S Barnes and Company at New York. Sidney Lee writes the introduction. Gordon Browne drew the pictures.

Lee opens with an old critics' quarrel. Does drama owe its excellence chiefly to plot or to character? Critics have waged that battle for two thousand years, he says. They rarely stay for a clear answer. To the plain observer, both plot and character are essential. In Shakespeare's best plays the two balance so evenly that only the short-sighted would rank one above the other. A plate shows Romeo's last embrace at page two hundred and forty-two. Macleod's tales gave children the stories whole, in prose they could follow. The book stands in the line of Lamb's Tales.
49339-graded-literature-readers-fourth-b:
The Fourth Book of the Graded Literature Readers was edited by Harry Pratt Judson, president of the University of Chicago, and Ida Bender, supervisor of primary grades in the Buffalo public schools. Merrill of New York copyrighted it in 1900. A picture of the sea fight between the Serapis and the Poor Richard leads the volume.

The contents grade upward from fairy tale to classic. The Straw, the Coal, and the Bean from Grimm opens the book. Hawthorne gives The Snow Image and a life of Newton. Carroll gives Alice with the kitten and The Walrus and the Carpenter. Alcott's Tilly's Christmas, Longfellow's Hiawatha's Sailing, and two psalms stand in the middle. Prince Ahmed from the Arabian Nights and Ruskin on nests fill the later pages. Schoolchildren of 1900 met the canon here, a few pages at a time.
503-the-blue-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang edits this first of his colored fairy books, gathering tales from France, Germany, and the East. Cinderella, Beauty and the Beast, and Aladdin sit beside Hansel and Gretel, Little Red Riding Hood, and Rumpelstiltskin. The Bronze Ring, East of the Sun and West of the Moon, and the Forty Thieves add rarer fare.

Lang retells each tale in clear, lively prose for children, keeping wonder and a touch of fear. The volume set the pattern for his whole series. It endures as a treasury where old tales meet new readers, and where a glass slipper still fits after more than a century.
50613-my-short-story-book:
A set of short tales for the young fills this book, one of a run of like books at one price and in one style. Its kin in the run are named on the first leaf. They are books of tales of the word of God, of wild beasts, and of the farm yard. Books of rhymes and of tales for the cradle room stand with them. Olive Molesworth, E. Nesbit, and L. L. Weedon are the chief hands in this book, with more names by them.

The list of parts gives the cast of the fare. The Snow Witch stands at its head, by Louisa Molesworth. A punch at a tree of the Christ feast, a kind pedlar, a lost doll, and a guest who was not asked come in its train. E.
51092-rattle-ok:
Harry Warner Jr wrote a comic tale first printed in Galaxy in December 1956. A note at the front jokes that a time machine might best serve store complaints. The tale opens at a wild Christmas party at a Boston store branch. Fast new drinks, rough games, and spilled tales set the rowdy scene.

A clerk in the mail order side of the house stands apart from the fun. A famed portrait of founder H H Hartshorne falls and cracks in the fray. Staff hide the glass and turn back to drink and play. Warner builds farce from pride, drink, and office rank before the time trick starts.
51248-the-library-of-entertainment-handb:
The Library of Entertainment Handbook guides owners of a home reading set. John Chilton Scammell wrote the handbook. Shuman published it at Chicago and Boston in 1920. The copyright dates to 1915. The set promised a thousand hours of enjoyment with the world's great writers.

Scammell's opening states the problem the book solves. Tired men and women ask where to find something worth reading. The handbook answers with notes on great writers and their oddities. A second part treats the study of literature. It covers decisive periods and national traits. A third part gives short studies of authors. Burns, Scott, and Wordsworth lead the list. Homer, Dante, Shakespeare, and Goethe appear as well.
51952-a-journalist-s-note-book:
A Journalist's Note Book, by Frank Frankfort Moore, was printed by Hutchinson in London in 1894. Moore also wrote Forbid the Banns and Daireen. Chapter one, Past and Present, opens with a wine auction anecdote. A publican buys the odd lots at a great collector's sale. He stirs Larose, Johannisberg, and Sauterne into one cask, unsure whether the mixture should be port.

These odd lots of journalistic experience, Moore says, may be considered a book, but he is not sure. His theme is the trade itself: journalists, he jokes, are all respectable nowadays, members of a recognised profession who may pronounce on art, taste, religion, morals, and even finance. The chapter heads promise talk of reviewing, of reading for pleasure against reading to criticise, and of the deterioration of literature.
52232-a-bible-hand-book:
A Bible Hand-Book, theologically arranged, was compiled by Holliday, a minister, and published at Cincinnati by Hitchcock and Walden in 1869. Its full title promises proof-texts on the leading doctrines of the Bible, set out so a reader can find them fast. Holliday says the work grew from spare hours snatched from an active pastorate in Indianapolis.

The handbook is divided into books, chapters, and sections, each doctrine proved by lines of Scripture. Book One treats doctrines relating to God: his existence, unity, eternity, power, presence, knowledge, wisdom, goodness, holiness, and justice. Later books take up the persons of the Godhead, with the Ten Commandments printed at the head of Book Four's chapters. Holliday meant it as a time saver for Bible students, young ministers, and Sunday school teachers.
52396-the-mary-frances-knitting-and-croc:
The Mary Frances Knitting and Crocheting Book, published at Philadelphia in 1918, is Jane Eayre Fryer's story-method for teaching girls to knit. Jane Allen Boyer drew pictures, and photographs show real work. Mary Frances learns among the Knitting People, where her tools talk. Crow Shay speaks for crochet, and Wooley Ball tells yarns of his own.

Lessons hide inside the adventures. Mary Marie, the doll, comes to life and needs a whole wardrobe. Chapters teach casting on, the knit stitch and the purl. Patterns make a doll's hood, sleeveless sweater, shawl, turban and teddy bear suit. Two more sweaters and a sports sweater follow. The last chapter turns the new skill to Red Cross knitting.
52747-baptism-as-taught-in-the-bible-and:
Baptism as Taught in the Bible and the Prayer Book is a doctrinal tract by Edward Hoare, incumbent of Trinity Church at Tunbridge Wells. The sixth edition came out in London from Hatchard and Company in 1865. A verse from the first epistle of Peter stands at its head. It bids the reader be ready to give a reason for his hope, with meekness and fear. Hoare owns at the start that few subjects have raised more controversy than baptism. He turns at once to the books themselves.

The Bible claims precedence in his court. Two questions frame the work. What inward blessing does Scripture join to the sacrament? And what is the nature of that joining? His answer sums the gifts as a saving union with Christ. The tract is a piece of the evangelical churchmanship of its age, plain and earnest.
52815-the-philadelphia-housewife-or-fami:
A cookery and household book by Aunt Mary. J B Lippincott and Company published it at Philadelphia in 1855. The preface argues a plain case. Family health depends on food more than on any other cause. Good advice must cover both the material and the preparation. Economy matters at every step.

Rich families often spoil fine ingredients with poor cooking. Poor families lack knowledge of cheap, nourishing foods. They also mistake heavy seasoning for good taste. Aunt Mary writes from long personal experience, at the request of many families. She adds kitchen order to her receipts. Every article belongs in its place, kept scrupulously clean. Exactness and timing complete the method.
52823-psychology-an-elementary-text-book:
Psychology, An Elementary Text Book, is a college text by Hermann Ebbinghaus, issued in 1908. Heath of Boston published the free translation by Max Meyer of Missouri. Ebbinghaus held the philosophy chair at Halle and edited a psychology journal. His fame rested on his pioneer memory studies, named on the title page.

Meyer preface praises the brevity and proportion of the material Ebbinghaus chose. The book keeps entirely free of all fads, the translator commends to students. A short course in sensation, memory, feeling, and will fills the compact volume. American classrooms gained German laboratory psychology in a teachable English form.
52910-pansy-s-sunday-book:
Pansy's Sunday Book gathers tales and verses for children from famous American writers. Lothrop Publishing Company issued it at Boston. Copyrights on the page run from 1886 to 1895. The book is fully illustrated.

The opening piece is a story in verse for late November. A speaker takes a child on his knee as snow falls outside. He tells of a poor lad from the city slums. The boy's head is brown and curly, his eye bright blue. His feet are bare and red, his trousers in shreds. The poem asks the listener to pity him, not judge him. Such Sunday books mixed story, song, and moral verse for family reading on the day of rest.
540-the-red-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang edits this second colored fairy book, gleaning less familiar tales from Norse, French, and German sources. The Twelve Dancing Princesses, Jack and the Beanstalk, Rapunzel, the Golden Goose, and the Story of Sigurd sit beside Drakestail, Mother Holle, and the Seven Foals. Translators, named in the preface, shaped each tale.

Lang hopes these tales, less worn than old friends, will charm anew. His clear prose keeps wonder without preach. The volume endures as a treasury for children and collectors, where a second gleaning proves the fairy field still rich.
54166-london-at-night-a-sketch-book:
Frederick Carter drew and wrote London at Night, a sketch-book published in London by Adam and Charles Black in 1914. The title page shows flower baskets being cleared away in Piccadilly Circus at 11 at night. Carter signed and dated his plates through 1913 and 1914.

A list of 24 plates maps the tour. Regent Street by night, Cleopatra's Needle, the Marble Arch, and a building scaffold lit in Oxford Street all appear. Other plates show electric light in the trees on the Embankment, Saint Paul's from the south, the arches under Charing Cross, and Hungerford Bridge. The book ends with the National Gallery from Trafalgar Square. Art lovers get the city after dark, in line and shadow.
54197-cambridge-a-sketch-book:
Cambridge: A Sketch-Book is a picture book of the university city by Walter Keesey. A and C Black published it in London. Its substance is a numbered set of drawings of Cambridge scenes. A view of the Trinity College fountain serves as frontispiece.

The plates move through the colleges and streets in turn. Clare College gates, bridge, and chapel views come early in the set. King's Chapel is drawn from outside and from its entrance. Trinity, Downing, and Sidney Sussex each receive their studies in turn. The round church of St Sepulchre contributes an interior view. Queen's College cloisters, gallery, and master's garden close the college tour. Street life enters with market day and the Saturday fish market. The Backs and Bridge Street complete a walker's portrait of the town.
54220-oxford-a-sketch-book:
Oxford, A Sketch-Book is a picture book of the university city by the artist Fred Richards. It was published in London by A and C Black in 1915. The text is made up almost wholly of the drawings themselves, each named in a list at the front.

There are twenty-four plates. They begin with Tom Tower at Christ Church and Carfax at the city centre. Colleges fill most of the list: Balliol, Trinity, Oriel, Merton, Magdalen, and Corpus Christi all appear. The Radcliffe Camera is drawn twice, from two colleges. Duke Humphrey's Library stands for the Bodleian. The set ends outdoors, with the river from Folly Bridge and a view of Oxford from the Hinksey path.
54315-cardiff-a-sketch-book:
Cardiff is a sketch-book of drawings by Andrews, issued by Black of London. Douglas Andrews drew the Welsh capital in twenty-four plates. City Hall on the title page sets the tone. The Bute statue and the newspaper offices follow. Saint Mary Street is seen from the old town hall. The castle is drawn twice, from two sides. Canton Bridge and Queen Street come next.

The library and the custom house are included. A coal-loading crane shows the port at work. The Bute docks, east and west, fill two plates. The canal and the law courts follow. The Welsh National Museum holds a captured German gun. Roath Park and Llandaff close the set. Llandaff Cathedral ends the book in two views. Such sketch-books sold the city's pride to visitors.
54317-isle-of-wight-a-sketch-book:
Isle of Wight: A Sketch Book is an artist's sketchbook of views on the Isle of Wight by Dorothy Woollard, published in London by Black in 1919. The book is a portfolio of drawings with almost no text: the island seen by a sketcher, place by place.

The list of sketches makes the tour. Carisbrook Castle serves as the title page. Yarmouth Castle, its streets, its square, and the view from the Yar bridge follow. Cowes comes next: west Cowes from the east, the ships off Cowes, and the beach. Newport, the island's town, gives its market square, its cattle market, the Medina river, and its church. Ryde pier and sands, Seaview, Saint Helens, and Brading church carry the eye east. Shanklin, Godshill, Ventnor beach, the Undercliffe's windy corner, and Freshwater church close the circuit of the island's coast.
54318-the-english-lakes-a-sketch-book:
Gordon Home sketched the English Lakes for Black of Soho Square, London, in a series of sixteen pencil drawings reproduced in this volume. The Langdale Pikes from a garden on Windermere front the book. Windermere from Bowness, Dove Cottage at Grasmere, and the stone circle near Keswick follow. Derwentwater is drawn twice, from Friar's Crag and from Borrowdale.

Buttermere, Scale Force, and Ennerdale Water from Pillar Fell carry the eye west. Wastwater and the Screes, clouds on Scafell, and the Styhead Pass give the high fells their weather. Ullswater is seen from the summit of Helvellyn. The series, edited by Hardie, offered sketch books at half a crown: sixteen or more reproductions, an artistic cover, and a district to carry in a coat pocket. Home, who sketched Malta and Stratford for the series, draws the Lakes as walkers of his day loved them, water below and tops above.
54324-stratford-on-avon-a-sketch-book:
Gordon Home made Stratford-on-Avon, a sketch-book of Shakespeare's town, for Adam and Charles Black of London. The illustrations run to 24 plates, and the monumental bust of Shakespeare serves as the title page picture. The book is a walk through the town with a pencil.

The plates take the sights in order. High Street and Holy Trinity Church come first, then the Birthplace and the birth room inside it. The guild hall and grammar school follow, with the site of New Place. The Memorial Theatre shows from the churchyard wall, and Clopton Bridge crosses the Avon. The Harvard House gets two plates. Anne Hathaway's cottage closes the set, and the home of Mary Arden ends the list. Pilgrims got the town's shrines in drawings they could carry home.
54326-the-thames-a-sketch-book:
Sharpley drew The Thames, a sketch-book for Black at London. Twenty-four sketches make the set, each named for its river place. Henley-on-Thames fronts the book as title page. Strand-on-the-Green, Key Bridge, and Ferry Road at Twickenham come early in the list. Kingston shows an old curiosity shop, and Hampton Court follows in its turn.

Sunbury, Walton Bridge, and the view below Staines Bridge fill the middle reach. Windsor Castle and bridge, Bray village, and West Street at Marlow come next. An old inn at Hurley, house-boats at Henley, and Sonning from the bridge pass by. Mapledurham mill, Goring bridge, and Streatley mill lead upriver. Wallingford, Shillingford bridge, Dorchester abbey's south door, Abingdon bridge, and Iffley close the set. The Thames unrolls here in pencil views from London's edge to Oxford's door.
54327-winchester-a-sketch-book:
Gordon Home drew Winchester, a sketch-book for Black at London. The house stood in Soho Square, the title page says. Twenty-three drawings make the set, each named for its place. The West Gate opens the list, then the city cross in the High Street. The west front of the cathedral and its cloisters follow.

The deanery and tower, the close gate, and the Norman clerestory come next. The font, the Norman arches, and the cathedral nave fill the middle. Chamber court and the cloisters of Winchester College take two plates. Catherine's Hill, Cross church from the river, and a hospital window follow. The old rectory, the mill, and a house called God Begot stand late. The castle hall and its round table close the set. Home gives the old capital in pencil views.
54328-york-a-sketch-book:
Gordon Home drew and wrote a sketch book of York for A and C Black in London. The form shown was issued in the spring of 1922. Sixteen plates show gates, streets, churches, and the great Minster. Martin Hardie shaped the wider set of town sketch books.

Views take in Micklegate Bar, St Mary's Abbey, and Clifford's Tower at York Castle. The Shambles, Stonegate, and the Guildhall door show the old town's charm. Each plate is drawn in pencil and shown in soft print form. Walkers and art fans gain a calm tour of one of England's most storied towns.
54336-bath-and-wells-a-sketch-book:
Bath and Wells is a sketch book of drawings by Andrews. Black of London issued the picture volume from Soho Square. Twenty four drawings list the Roman Bath, Guildhall, and Abbey at Bath first. High Street, Saint Michael Church, and Pulteney Bridge follow in the Bath set.

The mineral water fountain, Victoria Memorial, and Beau Nash house doorway appear. Bath from Beechen Cliff and from Alexandra Park give wide city views. Wells takes the second half: cathedral, market place, and Bishop Eye gate. The Chain Gate, Vicar Close, and Bishop Palace close the Wells drawings. Tor Hill gives the last wide view of Wells Cathedral here.
54344-bristol-a-sketch-book:
Bristol: A Sketch Book is a set of drawn views of the great west port by Woollard, who signs with one name plus marks. It came out at London from a house of art books. A list at its front names each sketch in its true rank.

A famed old church of the knights heads that list as the title page. Then come a poor house of the old town, a church lane, and a tailors court. In the arcades, at the flower mart, and at a famed old inn of a king street fill the next run. The great red church gets two views, its south door one of them. The docks, the great church walks, and the high bridge close the span.
54355-harrow-a-sketch-book:
Walter Keesey made a sketch book of Harrow in drawn views. The book came out in London in 1914. A church view serves as its title page plate. The list names more than a score of views in the set. High Street and the Old Schools lead the drawn walk.

The Fourth-Form Room shows twice, from two close views. The Terrace, the school chapel, and Pope's House come next. The Vaughan Library's in room and the head's yard front stand there. A head boy's den and the Byron tomb add odd charm. Eve on the terrace closes the set in soft light. School past fans get Harrow stone by stone.
54492-chester-a-sketch-book:
Chester: A Sketch-Book is a book of drawings of the city of Chester by Joseph Pike. It came out from A. and C. Black in London. A list of the sketches stands at the front and gives the whole plan of the book. The title page sketch shows King Charles' Tower. Then come Foregate Street, the cathedral from the city walls, and the cathedral cloisters.

More sketches show the town hall and Northgate Street, the canal and its Bridge of Sighs, and the Water Tower. The old Dee bridge, salmon boats on the River Dee, and Chester Castle stand in the list. Old houses, inns such as the Falcon and the Bear and Billet, and the famed Rows of Chester fill out the set as shown. The book is a tour of the city in pictures.
54734-tales-of-laughter-a-third-fairy-bo:
Kate Douglas Wiggin and Nora Archibald Smith edit a third fairy book of funny tales, issued in New York in 1908. The volume belongs to a Library of Fairy Literature, after The Fairy Ring and Magic Casements. A verse at the front bids the child reader write a name in the book before reading the first tale to its end.

Tales come from many lands, with thanks to publishers for tales from the field, from China, Sweden, Russia, and the far North. Grimm and Andersen stand beside Spanish and American Indian tales in the gathering. Reynard the fox, Bruin the bear, and Chanticleer the cock recur in piece after piece. Young readers get short, merry tales chosen for laughter rather than fright or tears.
55935-the-municipal-and-sanitary-enginee:
H Percy Boulnois, borough engineer of Portsmouth and late city surveyor of Exeter, wrote this handbook for municipal and sanitary engineers, published at London in 1883. Its motto is salus populi suprema lex: the people's health is the highest law.

The preface explains that in carrying out a borough surveyor's duties he often wished for a practical book of reference, and wrote one. The contents open with the town surveyor himself: his legal appointment under the Public Health Act, the examinations of the Sanitary Institute, and his duties in consequence. Traffic follows, with tables of resistance and the wearing effect of horses' hoofs. Boulnois also wrote on dirty dust-bins and the annihilation of sewer gases. Victorian surveyors get their whole office in one volume.
5615-the-pink-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang edited The Pink Fairy Book, gathering nursery tales from around the world. His preface notes that all peoples tell such tales to children. Japanese, Chinese, Native Americans by camp fires, Eskimo in winter huts, and South Africans join modern Greeks and old Egyptians, along with Germans, French, Spanish, Italians, Danes, and Highlanders. Stories resemble one another everywhere, Lang observes.

Children who read the Blue, Red, and Yellow Fairy Books will meet old friends with new faces here, alongside fresh tales. Lang's collection favors wonder, wit, and brevity. Readers get a classic fairy book, perfect for reading aloud, with tales gathered across continents.
56170-the-surprise-book:
Patten Beard wrote a children's book printed at Boston and Chicago in 1918, with pictures by Alice Beard. Beard had written The Jolly Year, The Bluebird's Garden, and The Good Crow's Happy Shop. Marjorie might hold the lantern and he'd see what was there, a picture says from page one hundred sixty seven. The book is given to Nall Candler, a young friend of her earlier books.

The surprise book that Dotty made opens the set. A surprise for each month follows: the telephone Santa Claus for December, the penny bank window for January, Angelina's valentine for February. Buttinski the peacemaker, Angelina's bird flower, and Marjorie's mystery fill the spring. Arne's Fourth of July battle, the blackberry adventure, Betty Crusoe, and the magical circle round the year. Cold and snow made Marjorie's own surprise book possible, the tale says.
56315-texas-fossils-an-amateur-collector:
William Matthews writes Texas Fossils, an amateur collector's handbook from the Bureau of Economic Geology at the University of Texas at Austin. It is guidebook 2, first out in November 1960. Printings run on to a ninth in August 1984, which shows its long use.

Early heads ask what fossils are and sort their study in three branches, plus the study of small forms. Long heads treat how fossils are kept: soft parts, hard parts, and stone swaps of lime, flint, and iron. Traces, molds, tracks, and dung stones each get a place. Later heads tell where to look, what kit to take, and how to clean a find.
56710-venomous-arthropod-handbook:
Venomous Arthropod Handbook, by Terry Biery, is a United States Air Force manual. Biery was a captain at the School of Aerospace Medicine, Brooks Air Force Base, Texas. The Government Printing Office issued it in 1977. Its subtitle lists four aims: symptoms and treatment of stings and bites, identification, biology, and control. Contents split the pests by kind. Biting and piercing sorts come first: black widow, brown recluse, centipedes, kissing bugs, and the wheel bug. Stinging sorts follow: ants, bees, scorpions, velvet ants, and wasps.

Blister beetles and stinging caterpillars close the main text. Each entry gives marks for knowing the creature, its range, and its habits. The black widow entry describes her red hourglass mark and ground-level web. Charts at the back cover drug treatment and shock.
571-the-1995-cia-world-factbook:
The Central Intelligence Agency's 1995 World Factbook surveys every country and territory in one reference volume. Entries run from Afghanistan to Zimbabwe, with notes on geography, people, government, economy, transport, communications, and defense forces. A search scheme lets readers jump straight to a country or a single category.

The Factbook's plain, tabular style makes it a quick check for basic facts as they stood in 1995. Borders, capitals, and economies have shifted since, so it serves best as a snapshot of its year. Researchers still value it as a baseline for how the world looked just after the Cold War.
57148-cigar-box-dioramas-a-how-to-do-it-:
Arminta Neal wrote a how to handbook on cigar box dioramas, copyrighted in 1958 and reprinted in 1961. Contents run from box preparation and background to foreground blocks and figures. A supply list opens the booklet: cigar boxes, scissors, a small knife, rubber cement, glue, black construction paper, and index cards.

Balsa wood or styrofoam, twigs, sifted sawdust, dyes, lichen, gravel, and sand are also apt to be needed. The box may open up, down, or to one side, with its main label pasted inside the lid. Later pages teach rocks, caves, bushes, ferns, water, trees, smoke, and snow. Neal wrote for hobbyists and teachers making small displays.
57896-luncheons-a-cook-s-picture-book:
Luncheons, a cook's picture book, published by the Century Company in 1902 as a supplement to the Century Cook Book, illustrated with over two hundred photographs. Its author explains that no general rules are given, since the parent book holds them.

Instead, dishes are listed by course at the head of each section, so a housekeeper can make up a menu at a glance. The early chapters cover garnishing, dishing butter, and the pastry-bag, then fruits, oyster and clam cocktails, and canapés. Soups and eggs follow as second and third courses. Garnishing gets real attention: pretty dishes, the book argues, recommend themselves, while careless ones are refused on appearance. Cooks get a photographed course-by-course repertoire.
58231-battles-bivouacs-a-french-soldier-:
Jacques Roujon wrote a French soldier's note book, translated by Fred Rothwell and first published at London in 1916. A comic song about La Ramée, a grenadier of Champagne, heads the book in French. Contents begin at Humes. In Lorraine, at the depot, and en route follow. A backward glance treats the battle of the Marne.

Before Fontenoy and our first trenches come next. Twenty two days in the trenches forms the longest chapter. A lull, bombardments, and Christmas follow. The Crouy affair closes the contents. Roujon's diary begins Tuesday, August 11, in the war's first days. Allen and Unwin issued many such soldier accounts.
58598-another-brownie-book:
Another Brownie Book is a picture book of verse by Palmer Cox, in an edition of 1890. A bookplate page at its front carries the Brownie Jury verdict for the owner. We, the Brownie Jury, do unanimously find that this book is the property of the child named there. 

Cox Brownies are a crew of little folk, each in the dress of some nation or trade in his drawings. They swarm through his pages in verse, building, sailing, and tumbling by night while the world sleeps. This second book gives them fresh adventures in the same jigging verse and crowded pictures. Cox, a Canadian in New York, built a small empire on the Brownies, who marched from his pages onto toys, games, and the first famous camera to bear their name for children.
58937-the-mary-frances-sewing-book:
Jane Eayre Fryer wrote The Mary Frances Sewing Book, or Adventures Among the Thimble People. The John C Winston Company issued it in Philadelphia in nineteen hundred thirteen. Jane Allen Boyer drew the pictures. Fryer had first sent Mary Frances to learn cooking from talking pots.

Now the girl spends a summer break at her grandmother’s house. There she meets the Thimble People, small folk of the work basket. Sewing Bird, a true fairy lady, leads the crew. They teach her seams and stitches as a game. A long trip to Thimble Land caps the fun. Girls learn to make pretty things as they read. Plain steps hide in tale form, so lessons land soft.
58948-flint-hills-cook-book:
Flint Hills Cook Book was compiled by women of Christ Church Parish. The parish at Burlington, Iowa, issued the cookbook in eighteen ninety five. Conrad Lutz printed and bound the volume in Burlington that year. Local ads for jewellers and cut glass houses front the book.

The preface begins with a custom hoary with the dust of ages. Church cookbooks of this kind gathered home recipes from parish kitchens. Readers get a community record of what Burlington families cooked and served. The book stands as a fund raising parish volume of its era. Its recipes preserve local tastes of the eighteen nineties in Iowa.
59734-daddy-s-little-rhyme-book:
Daddy's Little Rhyme Book, number five of the Old Nursery Rhymes, was printed in England with pictures by Willebeek Le Mair. Dance to your daddy leads the contents, then ride a cock horse and curly locks. Girls and boys come out to play and a frog he would a wooing go follow. What are little boys made of and there was a little man stand in the roll.

You shall have a fishy on a little dishy when the boat comes in, the first rhyme sings. Ride a cock horse to Banbury Cross, to see a fine lady with rings on her fingers and bells on her toes. Curly locks, wilt thou be mine, thou shalt not wash dishes nor feed the swine, but sit on a cushion and sew up a seam. A little cock sparrow and hush a bye baby close a pretty nursery picture book.
59812-nursie-s-little-rhyme-book:
Nursie's Little Rhyme Book is a set of rhymes for the young child's lap. Its leaves hold the old songs of the nurse room of past days. A song of men who march in and out of town stands in the set. The dame who keeps the book gives no name to the work.

Humpty Dumpty sits on his wall and takes his great fall in rhyme. The king's men and the king's horse can not set him right in the verse. Here we go round the bush of fruit starts an other of the songs. Plates with no caps of their own break the print of the rhymes. The book is made to be sung and said by rote in the child's room. Short lines and oft sung tunes are the whole stock of the book.
59863-butchers-packers-and-sausage-maker:
Geo J Sayer compiled the Butchers, Packers and Sausage Makers Red Book, with copyright in nineteen thirteen, for Wolf, Sayer and Heller. The firm kept houses in New York, Chicago, Montreal, Hamburg, Sydney, and London. An index of recipes heads the book. Curing and sausage making are the two great sections. Page pairs give each recipe in English and German style layout.

Curing recipes treat hams and bacon, smoking, boiling hams, and sugar cured breakfast bacon. Pumping, dry salt meats, mess pork, spare ribs, and pickled hog tongues follow. Pickled pigs feet, corned beef, rolled corned beef, and dried beef close the cure side. Sausage recipes then run from liver sausage and Braunschweiger Leberwurst to blood sausage, tongue sausage, and head cheese. Pork sausage, wiener, bologna, cervelat, salami, and Polish sausage fill the rest. Butchers get a trade recipe bible.
60904-a-book:
A Book, by Djuna Barnes, is a set of tales and poems issued in New York in 1923. Boni and Liveright held the copyright, and Barnes gives the book to her mother. Portrait drawings by the author serve as plates.

The first piece, A Night Among the Horses, opens toward dusk in summer. A man in a frock coat and top hat, cane in hand, creeps through brush at the edge of the Buckler farm corral. His knees are green from the shrubs, and he rests often, always guarding his hat. Dew falls on the leaves like damp faces, and a grove of white birches shines like teeth in a skull. Other pieces bear plain, odd names: The Valet, To the Dogs, Oscar, and The Flowering Corpse. Poems close the set, ending with Finis.
62472-aviation-book:
Aviation Book is a picture tale of flight for boys, told as a story. Two brothers who are boy scouts learn of air craft from their uncle. That uncle is a famed flyer whom the boys call Uncle Sam. The book bears a rights line of the year nineteen eighteen.

Prints show the first Wright plane as flown at Kitty Hawk in past years. The uncle tale walks the boys through parts, lifts, and risks of the air. Scout rank marks set Tom as new and Jack as more well versed. Bright chat aims to spark a wish to fly in young readers. The book rode the fame of flight in the last year of the great war.
62790-young-folks-nature-field-book:
Alden Loring wrote the Young Folks' Nature Field Book, published in Boston by Dana Estes and Company in 1906. Loring had served as field naturalist to the Biological Survey and the National Museum at Washington, and as curator of mammals at the New York Zoological Park. A photograph of a white-breasted nuthatch on a bird-house opens the book.

The publishers state the plan: a short, timely nature story or seasonable hint for every calendar day of the year. Each entry tells the reader when to look for each bird, beast, and flower, and how to know it when found. Pictures help with the naming, and every other page is left blank for the reader's own notes. Young naturalists got a year's worth of walks laid out by the calendar, with space to write their own book inside the book.
63055-gel-it-easy-ways-to-be-a-spectacul:
Gel It is a cookery booklet on gelatine from the Knox firm. Its subtitle promises easy ways to be a spectacular cook at home. A modern guide to gelatine cookery, the cover calls the booklet. The educational department of Knox Gelatine at Johnstown, New York, issued it. A new thirty minute gel that sets clear and airy stars it.

Readers design their own main dishes, salads, and desserts from patterns. Party snacks any day and diet and beauty tips fill more pages. Gel it in style, the first page cries, and add form to dishes. A shapely salad chills fast, and a refrigerator cake bakes without heat. What is gelatine follows: a granulated protein, colourless and tasteless.
6344-the-2002-cia-world-factbook:
The Central Intelligence Agency's World Factbook for 2002 lists every country and territory from Afghanistan to Zimbabwe, with oceans, islands, and disputed places in between. Each entry gives geography, people, government, economy, communications, transport, military, and transnational issues, in the Factbook's compact, factual style. A sample entry shows electricity by source, consumption, exports, and imports, with farm products, exports, and partners listed in figures.

Read as a whole, the volume is a reference snapshot of the world in 2002, before later borders, wars, and censuses changed its numbers. It is not a narrative but a tool, meant for quick lookup and comparison, from cocoa and gold exports to power grids and trade partners. The hosted file preserves that year's country listing in full, a useful baseline for anyone tracing how nations changed after it.
63748-mary-boyle-her-book:
Mary Boyle: Her Book was published by John Murray of London in 1901, edited by Sir Courtenay Boyle. Mary Boyle, who signs herself Vanessa, gives the pages to her cousins Gertrude, Countess of Kenmare, and Lady Sarah Spencer. Her nephew the editor says she left the choice of printing to those whose judgment she trusted.

The sketches were begun only a few years before her death, and he left them near as she wrote them. She flits, he says, like a butterfly from flower to flower, and jumps across wide gaps of years in a page or two. As a girl she shared in court life at home and abroad. Later she knew the leading literary men of the day, and she dwells with pride on her love of the drama and the dance.
640-the-yellow-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang edits this Yellow Fairy Book, fourth in his colored series after blue, red, and green. The Cat and the Mouse, the Six Swans, the Emperor's New Clothes, the Golden Crab, and Thumbelina lead the set, with the Steadfast Tin Soldier, the Tinder-box, and the Nightingale. A dedication to Joan, Toddles, and Tiny fronts the book.

Lang answers critics of fairy books by appealing to a jury of children, who, he trusts, will acquit him. His prose keeps the tales bright and plain. The volume endures as a beloved treasury, where old tales meet new readers in yellow covers.
64092-the-christmas-dinner-from-the-sket:
Washington Irving's Christmas Dinner, drawn from The Sketch Book, was issued on its own by William Edwin Rudge at New York in 1923. Verses from Withers's Juvenilia head it, calling every man to be jolly, with ivy on the rooms and holly on the posts. The sketch gives the great set piece of Irving's English Christmas.

The dinner is served in the great hall where the squire always holds his Christmas banquet, before a blazing fire of logs. The crusader's picture and arms are wreathed in holly and ivy, though the narrator doubts their age. A sideboard of plate accumulated through generations of jovial housekeepers glitters under two Yule candles. Minstrelsy from the old harper ushers in the company, and Irving studies the assembled faces like a collection of Holbein's portraits, finding antiquarian lore in the physiognomies of former times.
641-the-violet-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang edits this Violet Fairy Book, stressing in his preface that he did not invent these tales. Translated from folk tales in many tongues, they tell of the Tontlawald and the finest liar in the world. Three wonderful beggars, the goat's ears of Emperor Trojan, and the maiden with the wooden helmet add more wonder. Old magic stands where science now stands.

Lang writes that such tales are as old as human invention, told by savage mothers to savage children and later dressed with kings and queens. His clear prose keeps their wonder. The volume charms as a treasury of rarer fairy tales, where beasts talk and heroes learn by wit.
64916-riverside-london-a-sketch-book:
Riverside London is a sketch book by Dorothy Woollard and Boxer, published in London by Black. Its whole content is a set of twenty four drawings of the Thames side. The list of sketches opens with London Bridge as the title page view. Lambeth Bridge, Waterloo Bridge, and Cleopatra's Needle follow in order down the river.

Saint Paul's appears three times, from the river and from Waterloo Bridge. Bankside, Old Swan Wharf, and Fishmonger's Hall show the working river in the book. Cannon Street Station, Tower Bridge, and the Tower cover the city reach. The Pool and the docks near Limehouse show ships and trade on the water. The last views run down to Greenwich and Blackwall Reach at low tide. Each sketch stands alone as a plate with its title.
65429-sunset-s-cabin-plan-book:
Dillon put out a plan book for camp cabins from Sunset Magazine. The book's rights date to 1918 from Lane Publishing. Gordon drew its plates, and Friedell drew the house views. How to pick a site leads the book's list of themes. Water and clean needs for a camp come next in line.

Base work, fire hearths, and log walls each take a part. Stone and frame cabins and beach houses fill more pages. Thirty full plans run from page 21 to page 48. Camp tricks and spare gear close the book with a book list. West folk in that age built such camps by the score. Clear plans make the work a glad task.
6576-the-bobbsey-twins-at-meadow-brook:
Laura Lee Hope sends Nan, Bert, Freddie, and Flossie Bobbsey home from a fine trip, then off again for a summer at Meadow Brook. A crash of crockery opens the fun, and soon the twins face a runaway boy, a lost dog, a picnic, and a haystack hide-and-seek. The chapter list reads like a summer diary, full of small mishaps and quick rescues.

A sham battle, moving pictures, a circus, and a wild animal scare keep the pace lively, while a tale from a boy named Frank ties the loose ends. Hope keeps the talk bright and the danger mild, so young readers can enjoy the scare without fear. The Bobbsey Twins at Meadow Brook is a cheerful summer book for the youngest readers.
65863-on-the-border-with-crook:
John G Bourke, captain in the Third Cavalry, wrote On the Border with Crook. Charles Scribner's Sons published it at New York in 1891. A portrait of General George Crook fronts the book. Bourke inscribed it to Francis Parkman, whose pen had lit the history and wonders of the Great West. The volume describes the trials of the officers and enlisted men of the regular Army. They did much, he says, to conquer and develop the empire beyond the Missouri.

An old army saw opens the preface: you can never know a man until you have scouted with him in bad weather. Privation and danger bring every quality to the surface, Bourke writes. The comrade most popular at the post may come home lowered in all men's eyes. Bourke served under Crook in the Apache country.
66234-the-abergeldie-winter-book:
Mademoiselle Riego de la Branchardiere wrote The Abergeldie Winter Book, printed in London in 1867 at one shilling. She signs herself artiste in needlework, by special appointment, to the Princess of Wales. Prize medals of 1851, 1855, and 1862 are shown, awarded for the skill displayed in copying old Spanish and other costly laces. A front picture shows a cape, muff, cross-over, veste, petticoat, and hood.

The first pattern is an opera hood, in crochet, trimmed with tatting. Its stuffs are listed: skeins of pink and white single Berlin wool, and white floss silk, with a named tricot needle. The tatting calls for a large shuttle and two meshes of set sizes. The crown begins with the white wool and a chain of fifteen stitches, worked very loosely. Row by row the shaping is given, out to fourteen loops, then worked plain, then narrowed again.
66511-the-curtiss-aviation-book:
Glenn Curtiss and Augustus Post wrote The Curtiss Aviation Book, published in New York by Frederick Stokes. Other airmen add chapters: Captain Beck of the army, Lieutenant Ellyson of the navy, and Hugh Robinson. A photograph shows Curtiss flying the Hudson over the Statue of Liberty. The book is dedicated to Mabel Bell, who made the Aerial Experiment Association possible.

Three parts divide the story. Post tells the boyhood: motorcycle racing, and Baldwin's balloon. Curtiss then tells his first flights in his own words. The June Bug wins the Scientific American trophy, and the first water flights follow. The third part covers the chief flights: the Rheims meet, and the flight down the Hudson from Albany to New York. Air-minded readers got the pioneer's own log, from bicycles to the river flight.
6703-favorite-dishes-a-columbian-autogra:
Carrie Shuman compiles more than three hundred autograph recipes, with twenty-three portraits, from the Board of Lady Managers of the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago, 1893. The noble women behind the Women's Department gave these recipes so the compiler could help women pay the costs of a visit to the fair. Each dish bears its giver's own hand.

The book thus serves as both a cookbook and a souvenir of a great fair, with famous names beside plain, usable dishes. Shuman congratulates the lady managers warmly in her preface. Favorite Dishes is a delightful, historic cookbook, full of 1890s taste and fair-time pride.
67144-the-hole-book:
Peter Newell made this hole book, a picture tale in verse. Harper printed it in New York in October 1908. Tom Potts fools with a gun and it goes off bang. He did not know it was loaded, the verse says.

The bullet smashes a fine French clock just struck three. It bores through the wall and a kitchen boiler next. Bridget Quinn flees the flooded, steamy kitchen with a scream. Sister Sue swing rope is cut in the back yard scene. An artist laughing boy canvas takes the ball and changes its face in the tale.
6745-miss-parloa-s-new-cook-book:
Maria Parloa, principal of the Boston School of Cooking, offers a guide to marketing and cooking, with pictures. Her preface recalls the Appledore Cook Book of nine years before, written after she saw so many failures and so much mortification from vague directions. Minute steps, she found in teaching, were what cooks truly needed.

This new book keeps that plain, exact method, with marketing advice added to recipes. Parloa writes as a teacher, not a show cook, and her aim is success at home. Miss Parloa's New Cook Book is a classic, practical American cookbook, still clear and useful today.
6746-the-grey-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang edits The Grey Fairy Book, with tales from Lithuania, Africa, Germany, France, Greece, and many other lands. Translators and adapters include Mrs. Dent, Mrs. Lang, Eleanor Sellar, and Miss Blackley. The Three Sons of Hali comes from a French Cabinet des Fées of the last century, with tales nested inside tales, like carved ivory balls.

Lang notes that folk tales mix a set of incidents in endless new patterns, like glass in a kaleidoscope. The grey volume thus offers fresh wonders for children who know the red, blue, and yellow books. The Grey Fairy Book is a rich, world-wide fairy collection, made for reading aloud.
68267-the-cross-word-puzzle-book:
Buranelli, Hartswick and Petherbridge selected and edited these puzzles, published by the Plaza Publishing Company in 1924. Fifty cross word puzzles, chosen as the best of thousands submitted to the New York World, fill the anthology. They appear here exclusively for the first time, the title page states in full.

A comic poem on the cross word puzzle, by Levy, opens the book at the front. For many years we have lived as man and wife, the poem begins in jest.
