Rolling pins and hurled platters keep romance green in Levy's verses, until the Sunday lamp brings the couple to a puzzle, in the year the craze swept America.
68446-the-soup-and-sauce-book:
Elizabeth Douglas wrote a small book on soups and sauces for home cooks. Grant Richards issued The Soup and Sauce Book in London, priced at two shillings. It stands first in The New Cookery Books, with cake and pastry volumes after. Clear soups, thick soups, purees, bisques, and broths fill the first half.

Stock is the base of all soups, Douglas writes at the start. A good stock must be clear and free of fat for fine soups. Porcelain-lined pans and a steady, slow fire get her first praise. Cooks gain plain, tested rules plus sauces for fish, roasts, fowls, and game.
68567-the-pudding-and-pastry-book:
The Pudding and Pastry Book, by Elizabeth Douglas, stands third in the New Cookery Books line from Grant Richards of London. Each book in the line cost two shillings in cloth. Douglas had also written the soup and sauce book and the cake and biscuit book.

General rules open the book, on how to measure flour, sugar, salt, and spice with care. Parts then sort puddings by kind, from milk puddings and boiled custards to baked custards and fruit dishes. Later parts treat pancakes, fritters, omelets, and hot puddings, then sauces, jellies, and creams. Pastry, open tarts, and American pies close the main set, with cream ices after. Cooks get exact weights, as four cups of flour to a pound, in plain form.
68867-the-unique-story-book:
The Unique Story Book is one issue of a tiny monthly magazine. Its house called the print the smallest magazine in the world. Five cents bought the May issue of the year eighteen ninety five. Tales in small type fill its few pages for the post trade.

One tale tells of three gems found in a raid in war time days. Two old horse men at a meal trade the tale of that find. A girls name brings the lost facts back to one mans mind. Old raids round a town in Tennessee frame the war tale core. The odd small print served fans who prized quaint things in the mail.
68909-the-auxiliary-cook-book:
The ladies of the Auxiliary Society of the Hebrew Sheltering Guardian Society of New York Orphan Asylum published a cook book in 1909, priced at fifty cents. The book was made for the benefit of their Cottage Fund. As the tender bud needs sunshine, air, and water, so the child needs kindness, love, and rich food of body and soul, Ludwig Bernstein writes at the front.

Where a mother's love is taken away, those who stand in her place must be fired with her deep love, he says. The members gave their best and tried recipes with their signatures, the introduction owns, and took the greatest care in the work. Household hints add value to every home. Soups begin in cold water in iron or agate kettles, the rules say. Charity cooking here is plain, signed, and practical.
69345-the-mother-s-book:
L Maria Child wrote a guide for mothers on how to raise and teach young children. The sixth form, with fixes and new parts by the author, came out in New York. A long list of books from C S Francis and Company stands at the front. Child was known for The Frugal Housewife and for The Girl's Own Book.

The book holds that a child learns most from what parents do and say each day. Example, talk, work, and friends shape the child more than rules alone. Lines from Wordsworth and from Mrs Barbauld frame that view at the start. Parents of the time could use it as a plain, firm guide to home life.
69364-a-little-girl-s-cookery-book:
A Little Girl's Cookery Book is a cookbook for children, issued by Mills and Boon of London. Its front matter carries the publisher's list of general literature: stories of the British navy, of Westminster Abbey, and of the bee. Among such company the little cookery book takes its modest place. Its lessons begin with porridge.

When you are going to make porridge, it instructs, always begin to cook it the night before. A quart of boiling water goes in the outside of a double saucepan, and another quart in the inside. Plain rules of that sort fill the book, each fitted to small hands and a child's patience. The point is real cooking, not play cooking: breakfasts and plain dishes a girl could truly make and serve. The book belongs to the age that trained daughters at the stove early, and kindly.
69723-an-embroidery-book:
An Embroidery Book is a craft manual by Anne Knox Arthur of the Glasgow School of Art. It was published in London by Black in 1920. Sixteen full-page illustrations, eight of them in colour, go with the text. Eighty-seven line drawings stand in the pages as well. The author's note thanks the owners of the pieces shown. Students of the Glasgow school lent their work to be copied. A few pieces came from a school at Derby, worked by pupils there.

The book opens with an introduction on the craft and its history. Chapters then work through stitches, grounds, and designs in order. The Glasgow style, with its bold roses and clean lines, marks the pieces. The book was made for the student at her frame and for the teacher of needlework. Its plates let a worker copy fine models stitch by stitch.
70036-governor-william-bradford-s-letter:
Governor William Bradford's Letter Book reprints the letters of the Plymouth governor from a famed magazine. The Massachusetts Society of Mayflower Descendants published the reprint at Boston in nineteen o six. An opening note explains why so little known a work was reprinted for all. The original manuscript fragment can no longer be found, the note says.

The text follows a printing of seventeen ninety four in a historical society's volumes. A fragment of the letter book, covering sixteen twenty four to sixteen thirty, was found in Halifax. It turned up in a grocer's shop in Nova Scotia, of all places. James Clarke rescued it and gave it to the society in seventeen ninety three. Notes on that gift and on the manuscript's travels are reprinted in full.
70441-the-anzac-book:
The Anzac Book was published by Cassell in 1916. Men of Anzac wrote and drew it in Gallipoli. Its sale served patriotic funds of the corps. General Birdwood adds an introduction. A royal message heads the book: the troops had proved worthy sons of the Empire. The Landing opens the literary contents, told by a man of the Tenth. Poems and sketches follow in no set order. The Graves of Gallipoli and a lyre-bird poem stand near the front. From Quinn's Post and How I Shall Die speak from the trenches. Flies and fleas get their own comic piece.

Types of the force are drawn in words: Wallaby Joe, the Dag, and Bobbie of the New Army. The Indian Mule Corps and Hill 60 close the part shown. Humour carries the book's grief.
70517-the-glue-book:
J A Taggart wrote The Glue Book, a short guide for all who use glue. He issued the manual from Toledo, Ohio, in nineteen hundred thirteen. How to choose, make ready, and use glue is its whole theme. A modern glue testing room fronts the plain trade book.

Great waste rules the glue rooms of the land, Taggart warns at once. Sound judges hold that seventy per cent of glue is ill handled. True waste tops a fourth of all glue used, those judges add. Bad joints in fine work swell the loss past count, he says. Peter Cooper founded the trade in America, his first part shows. Boiling stock and drying it fill the next trade pages. Jelly tests and the plain finger test grade the goods for buyers. Plain words, not science terms, rule the whole shop wise book.
70574-little-jack-rabbit-s-big-blue-book:
Little Jack Rabbit Big Blue Book, by David Cory, collects bunny tales for children. Grosset and Dunlap issued it at New York with rights in 1924. Full page colour and black and white pictures crowd the big book. Cory signs himself the Jack Rabbit Man in a verse to readers upfront.

A note to grown ups invites them back to make believe land again. Talking dogs, rabbits in knickers, and birds in hollow trees feel natural there. Tales run from The Wedding and Hungry Hawk to the Lollypop Tree in fun. Radio alarms, a circus elephant, and Danny Fox fill the list of tales. Uncle Lucky dreams, races run, and valentines arrive across twenty eight stories.
71108-meadow-brook:
Meadow Brook is a novel by Mary Holmes, published at New York in 1858. Saxton issued it; the copyright was entered the year before. Holmes had written The Homestead on the Hillside and 'Lena Rivers. She dedicates the book to her mother. The preface owns that the story holds more truth than most of its kind. Rosa Lee's early home and childhood are mostly the author's own.

Holmes denies, though, that she simply made herself the heroine. The fickle Clayton and his haughty bride people the fiction. So do the unfortunate Herbert and the disappointed Ada. A proud Southern planter and gentle Jessie complete her gallery of American types. A friend's two years in Georgia supplied the Southern scenes. Holmes aimed at the probable rather than the wonderful.
71416-the-bible-object-book:
The Bible Object Book is a set of thing lessons by Clarence Herbert Woolston. A Judson press brought it out in August of nineteen twenty six. Its next line calls the lessons ones which are different from the rest. Woolston wrote Seeing Truth and the Penny Object Lessons in past years. He made the Seeing Truth packs of lessons and things as well.

The book is set for the boys and girls of Bethany Hall at Winona Lake. Those kids heard and saw these sight talks at that lake camp. A front word says no man fits this work more than Woolston does. He loves and knows kids, and heart is the core of the craft there. Twenty years of lake camp crowds back that claim in the note.
7223-the-belgian-cookbook:
Mrs Brian Luck edited this Belgian cook-book from recipes sent by Belgian refugees from all parts of the United Kingdom in 1915. She notes that British cooking may benefit from Belgian dishes, and she offers the small manual for the workaday and inexperienced mistress and maid, not for millionaires. The perfect cook, she jokes, is often heard of but never found.

Refugee kitchens thus become a quiet act of welcome, turning exile into shared tables and plain, good food. The recipes favour thrift and home skill over display, and the book's wartime origin gives its homely advice a deeper warmth. Readers get Belgian fare in English kitchens, gathered in a time of need.
72362-the-golden-story-book:
Ernest Nister of London and E P Dutton of New York issued this story book for the young, written by many hands. G Manville Fenn, D H Parry, G A Henty, Sheila Braine, and L L Weedon head the bill. Tales of war and daring fill the contents: How Jean Became a Soldier, Defending the Fort, and A Border Raid.

How a Drummer Boy Saved a Regiment comes from Henty, and The Jailer's Little Son from E Everett-Green. Lilian Gask tells of Jean-Pierre, the St Bernard dog. The first tale opens in June 1815, on a quiet farm near two armies making ready for a great battle. Little Jean le Grand trudges home worn out, while his father drinks with soldiers in the next village.
72426-lady-rosamond-s-book:
Lucy Ellen Guernsey wrote Lady Rosamond Book, or Dawnings of Light, issued in London by John F Shaw and Company in a new edition. Guernsey had earlier written Lady Betty Governess and Winifred. The book stands in the Stanton Corbet Chronicles and is set in the year fifteen twenty nine. Forty three chapters run into May fifteen ninety. A plate shows a girl climbing over a wall by the beehives.

Chapters are dated by feasts and days, like a diary of a Tudor girl. Feasts of Saint Agnes, Saint Catherine, and Saint John Baptist mark the year. Later entries take Rosamond to Corby End, Tremador in Cornwall, and Coombe Ashton. A preamble says the finder found the original of the book, dated seventeen ten, in a father library. Young readers get Tudor faith, home life, and peril in diary form.
72443-betty-crocker-picture-cooky-book:
Betty Crocker Picture Cooky Book, copyrighted by General Mills in 1948, gathers cookie recipes for home bakers. Its cover promises 128 of the most popular tested recipes from her collection. Seventy how to tips, fifty success pointers, and 175 illustrations go with them. Extra copies cost twenty five cents by mail from Minneapolis.

A letter to the reader calls the book the newest and fullest collection of cooky recipes from the firm. It answers thousands of requests from home cooks, that letter states in warm terms. Key symbols mark the important recipes in the original printing for quick use. Picture steps show each method for bakers who learn best by eye. The Betty Crocker name, a registered trade mark, fronts the whole General Mills test kitchen brand.
72483-the-vertigo-hook:
Richard Ashby's The Vertigo Hook comes from Fantastic Universe for October-November 1953. The editor's note bills it as a time story with a scramble not seen since Murray Leinster's Sidewise in Time, and promises a definite, unsuspected answer to who won the Civil War. Time here does not run on a single track; it may move in other directions as well.

The tale opens outside time altogether. The Irritant, hungry and ill-humoured in the cold voids, finds no flicker of edible consciousness for eons around. It baits a line with a tangled skein of thoughts about conflict, the hook a hard curve of sharpened vertigo, and trolls through the blankness of time. The scene then cuts to earth: Major Hall, in Air Corps blues, slides a sheaf of papers to Ed Wilkes, an honor graduate buried in a small southern college.
7277-the-green-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang's Green Fairy Book, the third of his coloured fairy books, follows the Blue and the Red, made because children kept asking for more. Lang tells his friendly reader that the stories are borrowed from many countries: some French, some German, some Russian, some Italian, some Scottish, some English, and one Chinese. However much nations differ about trifles, he writes, they all agree in liking fairy tales.

Men long ago, Lang suggests, were much like children in their minds, and that likeness keeps old tales alive across borders. The green volume gathers its wonders with the same generous hand as its sisters, for reading aloud at bedtime. It stands as a classic treasury of world wonder tales.
72966-the-horror-at-red-hook:
H P Lovecraft wrote The Horror at Red Hook, a tale shown here from Weird Tales in March 1952. A quote from Arthur Machen heads the tale. Machen speaks of rites of evil and of lore not yet dead. Part One opens in the village of Pascoag in Rhode Island.

A tall, stout, sound looking man comes down the hill from Chepachet. He turns into the main street with its small shops. He stares at the tallest building, shrieks in terror, and runs till he falls at the next crossing. Folk pick him up and dust him off. He is whole in body and cured of his fit, it seems. He mutters of a strain he had borne and turns back with downcast eyes. The tale then digs into the Red Hook horror behind his fear.
73388-the-gospel-object-book:
The Gospel Object Book is a teaching manual by the Reverend Clarence H Woolston. The Rodeheaver Hall-Mack Company published it, with copyright in 1925. Woolston dedicates it to the children of the Cedar Falls Bible Conference in Iowa.

The book gives object lessons for Sunday schools and children's meetings. Each lesson uses a visible thing to carry a Bible truth. The preface argues that children learn far more through the eye than the ear. Woolston says he spoke to over a million children this way. Object lessons were a core tool of revival era children's work. This manual shows the method lesson by lesson.
73744-the-royal-baker-and-pastry-cook:
The Royal Baker and Pastry Cook is a manual of practical cookery by the chefs of the New York Cooking School. The Royal Baking Powder company published the book in New York in 1902. An alphabetical index of receipts opens the book. Breads come first in force: brown bread in several forms, Boston brown, corn breads, graham breads, oatmeal, rice, and rye, then buns, biscuits, and bannocks.

Savory receipts follow: braised beef, corned beef and turnips, brown beef stew, beef tea, and broiled steak. Vegetables, soups, and invalid drinks such as barley water have their place. The manual is a maker's cookbook, built to put its baking powder to work in a full household kitchen. Measures and steps stay plain, in the manner of a cooking-school lesson.
73816-the-greedy-book:
Frank Schloesser gathered a food anthology in 1906, calling it a gastronomical anthology. He had already written The Cult of the Chafing Dish. Chapters range over cooks and cookery, the poet in the kitchen, and the salad in literature. One chapter is given to Mrs. Glasse and her hare, and one to menus.

Later parts treat oysters, waiters and snails, dishes of history, and Lenten fare. The opening quote from John Davidson praises eating and drinking as fine human arts. Schloesser thanks several London papers for leave to reuse pieces. The book suits readers who enjoy food writing with a literary bent.
74369-chinese-cook-book:
Vernon Galster wrote the Chinese Cook Book in Plain English, copyrighted in 1917 and published by the author at Morris, Illinois. The book sold for one dollar. Its cover promises recipes for chop suey, eggs fo young, war mein, yet ca mein, chow mein, and bird's nest soup.

Galster asks his opening question plainly: is this book for you? It is for the person a thousand miles from a Chinese restaurant, he says. It is for the camper, the clubman, and the wife who wants to surprise a husband who praises restaurant feeds. He promises the methods of the greatest Chinese chefs, and offers to supply the imported sauces and vegetables needed. The book is part cookery, part mail-order pitch, from the years when chop suey swept America.
75331-the-fireside-story-book:
The Fireside Story Book gathers three tales by Maria Edgeworth. Appleton published it at Philadelphia and New York in 1847. Edgeworth had earlier written Popular Tales and Moral Tales. The three stories are Waste Not, Want Not, The Bracelets, and Lazy Lawrence. Illustrations come from original designs.

The first tale states its lesson in its subtitle. It promises two strings to your bow. A Bristol merchant named Gresham retires to a new house near Clifton. Having no sons, he means to adopt a nephew. He invites both nephews to judge their habits. Hal learned waste in a rich household. Benjamin learned care from a poor father. The uncle watches the boys closely.
75448-dorothy-dix-her-book:
Dorothy Dix wrote Dorothy Dix Her Book, a guide to daily help for daily folk. The second form came out in New York and London in 1927, a year past the first. Dix was a famed voice whose short talks ran in the press. Her tone here is plain, warm, and full of good sense.

Short parts ask how a wife should treat a spouse, and what charm is. She tells girls to learn a trade, and wives to wed the man they love. Parts deal with envy, with drift in wedlock, and with how to stay young. Work, talk, and the rearing of young ones all get a turn. Fathers are asked if they are good ones, and if they sell their worth to their young. The book reads as a set of brisk talks on home life.
76069-pansy-s-home-story-book:
Pansy's Home Story Book, issued in Boston in 1896 by the Lothrop Publishing Company, gathers short tales for young readers at home. The book was edited by Mrs Alden, who wrote under the name Pansy. Its long table of contents names dozens of brief pieces, most of them set in homes, schools, and small towns.

Inside, five friends meet under an old tree at the end of summer and agree to tell the tales of their trips. Other pieces bear names like The Old Arm-Chair, Minnie Lee and Her Kitten, and A Letter From Bird-Land. Some tales are signed by other hands, among them the Reverend Alden and Margaret Sidney. The mix suits family reading aloud.
76300-lion-yarn-book:
Lion Yarn Book was issued by the Lion Yarn Company in 1920. Its cover shows the Lion Yarn Mill, where Lion Brand yarns are made. The mark stands for quality and full weight, the page claims. Patterns for the latest creations in worsted work fill the book. A skating set leads: a sweater with scarf attached. Materials are listed exactly: seven hanks of black knitting yarn, two of tango orange, and one each of green and red. Amber needles in two sizes and a crochet hook complete the kit. The colour order is spelled out band by band.

Black works four knit, four purl for fifteen rows; tango orange takes four. Green and red flash between black bands. Cuffs pick up fifty stitches at the sleeve end.
76322-the-kiltartan-wonder-book:
The Kiltartan Wonder Book is a set of Irish wonder tales retold by Lady Gregory, with pictures by Margaret Gregory. The book is given to a Kiltartan child, and the tales are told in the plain, musical speech Gregory made her own. Kiltartan was her home district in Galway, and its storytellers stand behind the page.

The contents open with The Mule, told by an old man who had promised a codfish and brought only a hake. Three sons of a dead king chase a singing bird, and the fool of the family pulls its tail and must follow it. Other tales tell of the seven fishers, King Solomon, the Danes, and a woman who was a great fool.
76498-evangelical-lutheran-hymn-book:
Concordia Publishing House issued this short form hymn book in Saint Louis in 1927. It holds the order of morning worship for Lutheran churches. The book gives the words for priest and flock to say and sing. It was made for use in the pew each week.

Pages lead from a call to prayer through confession and pardon. The flock then hears creeds, psalms, and hymns in set order. Clear print marks who speaks each part and when to stand. The book shows how one church shaped its shared praise in that era.
76611-khaki-knitting-book:
The Khaki Knitting Book is a wartime pattern book edited by Olive Whiting. It was copyrighted in 1917 by Allies Special Aid in New York. An opening poem urges knitters to knit their bit. Sweater, muffler, and sock are named as the goods. The foreword says the book is no teaching manual. Its patterns suit those who already know the craft.

The patterns make warm wear for soldiers at the front. Home knitters across America took up such work. Yarn firms and relief groups lent their directions freely. The Red Cross is among those thanked in the book. Money from sales went to the Allied cause. Lending the book to a friend was called a fraud on the Allies. Khaki, gray, and blue were the colours of the day.
76756-the-orkney-book:
John Gunn compiles The Orkney Book, readings for young Orcadians, from Nelson of London, Edinburgh, and New York. Gunn had writ Sons of the Vikings and The Boys of Hamnavoe. A poem by Duncan Robertson, Sons of the Isles, fronts the book with salt spray and northern stars.

His preface tells the book's birth. It is a book about Orkney, for use in Orkney, made and in most part writ by natives of Orkney. The Edinburgh University Orcadian Association first felt the need of it. Schools in the isles lacked a book fit for their own ground and seas. Teachers now hold that knowledge, like charity, should start at home, Gunn notes.
76850-the-watchmakers-hand-book:
The Watchmaker's Hand-Book is a trade manual for horologists, built in parts. Its first part covers arithmetic, geometry, and drawing, the base skills of the bench. It explains signs used in calculation, powers and roots, and proportion. Practical geometry and the use of drawing instruments follow.

The second part turns to the materials of horology, beginning with iron and cast iron. Later parts treat work in precious stones and the use of file and graver. The reader learns to file flat and square with both hands at once, and with one hand. Turning cylindrical pivots takes its own lessons. A micrometer dividing table and other methods of dividing into equal parts serve the fine work of the craft. The book is a complete bench companion for the Victorian watchmaker.
77776-of-the-making-of-a-book:
Of the Making of a Book, a few technical suggestions meant as aids to authors, was compiled by the literary department of Appleton and Company of New York in 1904. Two specimen proof sheets stand at the front, one showing the marks used in proof-reading, the other the same page corrected in the type. A life of William Falconer follows as reading matter.

Falconer, a barber's son from Edinburgh who went to sea, lost his ship in the Levant and made the poem The Shipwreck from the wreck. The chapters then do the book's own work: the manuscript, composition and the proofs, proof-reading, illustrations, and publicity. An index closes a short, plain guide for writers new to print.
7797-the-lady-of-the-aroostook:
William Dean Howells's The Lady of the Aroostook opens in the best room of a farmhouse in the hills of northern Massachusetts, one August morning. An elderly woman rocks in a haircloth chair, an old man drums stubbed fingers and whistles without sound, both dressed in unaccustomed finery.

His fresh-shaven face, black satin stock, and lead-colored straw hat mark a family preparing for a journey. The lady of the title will sail on the Aroostook, and Howells follows her from farm parlor to shipboard society, with his usual gentle comedy of American manners abroad.
78045-the-happiness-of-hazelbrook:
Happiness of Hazelbrook is a story by Charlotte O'Brien, billed as author of Harry Blake's Trouble. The hosted edition came from a London religious tract house. Its contents list seven chapters, from Duty and Pleasure to Safe at Home. A front picture shows a girl lying quite motionless.

Chapter one opens at home on a working morning. Mrs Lawrence is leaving for a day's washing at the rectory. She asks her daughter Katie whether the shirt in hand can be finished by evening. Katie says only the two sleeves and wristbands remain, and those are stitched already. Her mother promised the shirts for that night to a lady leaving Hazelbrook next day. Katie vows to sit steadily to work and not stir till it is done.
78121-the-servant-s-behaviour-book:
The Servant's Behaviour Book offers hints on manners and dress for maid servants in small households. Mrs Motherly wrote it under that pen name. Bell and Daldy published it in London in 1859. The author addresses her readers directly as dear girls. Every rule, she says, is necessary to a girl entering a gentleman's family.

Good manners, she argues, decide a servant's rise. Many a good servant stays in inferior places for want of them. Many a servant of small abilities advances through good breeding alone. Girls fear that new rules will make them noticed. Mrs Motherly answers that neglect, not obedience, draws eyes. One girl thought it ill-tempered to enter a drawing-room silently with a coal-scuttle. Another balked at carrying letters on a tray. Saying Sir and Ma'am at every sentence struck a third as foolish. The book patiently corrects each fear from the author's own service.
78335-the-limerick-up-to-date-book:
The Limerick Up-to-Date Book, composed and collected by Ethel Watts Mumford, is a calendar of limericks with a verse for the days of the year. Paul Elder published it at San Francisco in 1903. Mumford and Addison Mizner drew and decorated the pages.

Each opening gives a limerick, a page for notes, and the date rendered in many tongues and scripts: French, German, Spanish, Italian, Greek, Japanese, and Chinese among them. The January verses begin with good resolutions, as a hungover John swears off crackers for the year. A dame at the beaches of Florida proves horrider than the ladies said, and a flirtatious exchange follows under the head of Flattery. The book belongs to the limerick craze that swept America after Edward Lear's old nonsense verses found new life.
78583-utopia-yarn-book:
The Utopia Yarn Book, in its fourteenth edition, is a practical treatise on knitting and crocheting. The manufacturers of Utopia yarns published it, and the Frankenberg company of New York copyrighted it in 1919. Introductory remarks promise exceptionally novel ideas, embodying the very latest creations of sweater coats.

The charm of the garments, the makers argue, owes much to the yarns themselves: softness, elasticity, and evenness of thread, with a yarn for every purpose. To avoid the common error of directions too hard to understand, a well known expert wrote the instructions. Every standard stitch is illustrated, and directions run from the making of the stitch to the finished garment. The novelties interest the expert while the novice follows with ease. A long list of abbreviations follows, from stitch and border to skein and scallop, before the patterns begin.
78781-the-healthy-life-beverage-book:
The Healthy Life Beverage Book, by H Valentine Knaggs, was published in London in nineteen eleven by C W Daniel. Knaggs was a licentiate of the Royal College of Physicians and an author of dietetic pamphlets. His compilation is alphabetically arranged. It promises refreshing, curative, stimulating, and nutritive liquids of every kind.

The recipes cover fresh fruit and vegetable juices, vegetable broths, and cereal drinks. Unfired fruit soups, nut milks, plant teas, herbal decoctions, and fruit syrups all appear. Critical notes judge water, milk, whey, beef tea, vinegar, sugar, coffee, tea, and cocoa. Knaggs's foreword holds that modern bodies are clogged with waste and thirst for cleansing liquid. He answers that thirst with nature's drinks rather than the adulterated bottles of commerce.
79072-the-voter-s-text-book:
James Hiatt compiled The Voter's Text Book, printed at Indianapolis in 1868 by Asher, Adams and Higgins. The title page calls it a gathering of the chief papers and figures in America's past as a state, drawn from public records, with sketches of lives and events. A portrait of George Washington fronts it.

The papers run in order: the making of the first union, the Declaration of Independence, the Articles of Confederation, and the Constitution with its amendments. Washington's addresses follow, then the Missouri Compromise, the Fugitive Slave Law of 1850, and the Kansas and Nebraska Act. The Emancipation Proclamation stands near the end of the papers, and lives of the presidents, each with its vote count by term, fill the rest.
79268-a-cat-book:
A Cat Book is a book of light verses on cats by Lucas, issued at New York and London in 1927. Its pictures are by Pat Sullivan, the maker of Felix the Cat. A cat washing itself opens the picture list. The first verse treats the cat's daintiness at table. A cat that wants feeding has very little mind for bread, it says.

At thick or thin, at new or stale, she waves no thank you with her tail. But butter she would eat by the pat, such is the nature of a cat. Greediness follows: for milk a cat will do a hundred things she ought not, and for cream ten times as many. The cat's dream is a milk pail filled with cream, drawn fresh from the cow. Cleanliness and other cat traits get their verses in turn.
7935-ballad-book:
Katharine Lee Bates of Wellesley College edits Ballad Book. It opens with Wordsworth on plaintive numbers flowing for old, unhappy, far-off things and battles long ago. Her preface argues that teaching literature should first wake love and enthusiasm for poetry, since love guarantees wider study.

Early ballads, belonging to the youth of English literature and race, appeal with special power to youth, Bates says. Most men of letters keep a boy's tenderness for these rough, frank, spirited poems. The collection offers students a starting point in the critical study of English verse.
79370-ryzon-baking-book:
A baking book built around Ryzon, a branded baking powder. The book opens with social proof on a grand scale. New York's leading hotels, clubs, and restaurants adopted Ryzon early. The Waldorf-Astoria, Delmonico's, and Sherry's head the list. West Point and Annapolis messes appear as well. Master chefs, the text boasts, recognised its excellence quickly.

Recipe chapters follow the advertising front matter. Breads and quick breads come first, then cakes in loaf and layer forms. Cookies, doughnuts, pastry, pies, and puddings fill later chapters. Measuring directions promise to save eggs and money. A recipe contest's prize winners get their own pages. The volume shows how food brands taught American home baking. Every recipe quietly sells the powder in its title.
79432-the-chinook:
The Chinook is a novel of the timber country by Frank Richardson Pierce. Its teaser promises that all is fair in love and timber war, and that the timber baron Ludwig has badly reckoned his man. No publisher or date stands in the front matter shown.

Dan Todd of the Forest Service rides through a midnight downpour toward Black Lake cabin on his horse Chinook. Todd has bucked Sim Ludwig, the powerful and grasping timber owner, and been warned that no service man who does so keeps his place. He is riding out of the service into an unknown future. On a ledge of Flaming Falls Trail his torch catches a flash of gold: a girl's golden slipper, the last thing he expected there. The cougar country, the feud, and the slipper set the plot moving.
87-the-1993-cia-world-factbook:
The Central Intelligence Agency's 1993 Factbook arrived as a preliminary edition, rough in form but full in scope. A note warns that a neater final edition would follow around October 31, 1993. Redundancies were trimmed to cut storage and search costs.

Country entries still follow the agency pattern: geography, people, government, economy, communications, and defense forces. Afghanistan opens the alphabetical list as usual. The 1993 volume captures new states and shifting borders after the Soviet fall. It remains a working snapshot of a world remade. Its preliminary status makes it a telling record of how reference data reached readers then.
8890-mary-jane-her-book:
Clara Ingram Judson writes Mary Jane, Her Book, illustrated by Frances White, as a series of short episodes in a little girl's life. Contents include the broken doll, don't cry over spilled sugar, helping the robins, father's secret, Mary Jane plays school, and aunt Effie comes to visit. Kewpie and the washing, junior's shower bath, playmate Dorothy, learning to sew, and making ready for the picnic follow. The picnic up Clearwater, going shopping, the paper doll show, the birthday party, and a letter and a trip.

Illustrations catch Mary Jane with clinched fists and a perky plaid ribbon showing amazement, exclaiming over a paper doll that looks like her. Sitting on a rock by a creek. Judson's stories teach kindness, helpfulness, and good humour through everyday mishaps.
907-flying-machines-construction-and-ope:
W. J. Jackman and Thomas H. Russell wrote this practical book on how to build and navigate the modern flying machine. With illustrations, working plans, and plain text, they show the reader the frame, the engine, and the controls, and how a pilot handles wind, balance, and landing.

Jackman, author of books on motorcycling, and Russell write for the amateur builder, not the theorist, and their tone is direct and encouraging. The book captures the moment when flight passed from dream to workshop, and it still interests model makers and historians of early aviation for its plans and its can-do spirit.
9913-the-trail-book:
Mary Austin's 1918 book for children follows Oliver and Dorcas Jane as they find the trail through their own country, hoping it leads to wonderland. Along the way, storytellers explain how the world was made: a buffalo chief, Arrumpa with the mastodon, the coyote, and the corn woman.

Later tales tell of the salt trail, the Tallegewi, and how the Lenni-Lenape came from Shinaki, each tied to a real path across the land. Austin, with pictures by Milo Winter, joins Native American storytelling to American geography. Young readers get adventure, myth, and a map of trails under their feet.
a-chinese-wonder-book: Norman Hinsdale Pitman retells Chinese wonder tales in this illustrated book. Its stories include the golden beetle, the great bell, the strange tale of Doctor Dog, and how footbinding started. Other tales treat a talking fish, bamboo and the turtle, and a mad goose in a tiger forest. Pitman presents old Chinese lore in clear English stories for young readers.
a-florida-sketch-book: Bradford Torrey sketches Florida in a book of nature writing. Its chapters wander the flat woods, the marsh, the beach at Daytona, and the hills along the Hillsborough. A morning at an old sugar mill, the upper St. John's, and walks about Tallahassee follow. Torrey, approaching Jacksonville by rail through endless pine barrens, writes of birds and landscape with care.
a-kindergarten-story-book: Jane Lincoln Hoxie offers a kindergarten story book for young children. Many stories had been told to thousands of children in kindergartens from Boston to Pittsburgh. Their delight assures their appeal to child thought and sympathy. Hoxie inscribes the book to her father, whose evening story hour she remembers best.
a-pr-mvad-szok:
A prémvadászok, published in 1873, is the Hungarian translation of a tale by Jules Verne. Verne's adventure novels traveled fast across Europe, and Hungarian readers met many of them in versions like this one. The book preserves that Hungarian form, in which generations of readers in Hungary first followed Verne's northern adventure.

The story opens on the evening of the seventeenth of March, 1859, at Fort Reliance in the far north. Captain Craventy gives a small fête at the fort, a simple reception for which he has spared no pains. From that remote outpost gathering, the tale of fur hunters and the frozen country begins, in classic Verne fashion.
ballad-book:
Katharine Lee Bates of Wellesley College edited this school anthology of early ballads. Her preface speaks for teachers of English: the classroom is only the vestibule to education, and love of poetry is the surest guarantee of study beyond it. Ballads suit the start, she argues, belonging to the youth of the literature and of the English race. Wordsworth's lines on old, unhappy, far-off things stand as motto.

Texts follow in the old spellings, with battles and betrayals in every stanza. The Dowie Dens of Yarrow gives a sample. A lone fighter comes to wield his brand on Yarrow's banks. He hurts two men and slays three. Then a stubborn knight creeps in behind and pierces him through. Bates shaped generations of American schoolrooms' first taste of the traditional ballad.
britannica-1911-bangkok:
Bangkok is the capital of Siam, on the river Me Nam about twenty miles from its mouth. Until modern times the city stood largely on floating pontoons or on piles along its countless canals, which served as its streets. By 1911 well-planned roads crossed the canals at many points, lined with brick houses.

The royal palace, walled in a bend of the river, forms the centre. A second wall, nearly a mile out, rings the packed city proper, with royal parks to the north and the business quarter, rice mills, and docks to the south. The 1911 Britannica entry notes electric tramways, tree-lined streets lit by electricity, and Buddhist temples scattered all over with coloured tile roofs and gilded spires.
britannica-1911-chapbook:
Chapbook is a book article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about small stitched tracts sold to common folk. The name draws on an old English word for buying and selling. Travelling dealers, called chapmen, carried the tracts through England, Scotland, and the American colonies.

The article lists the stock tales of the trade. Tom Thumb, Jack the Giant Killer, and Dick Whittington head the roll. Tales of travel, lives of famed folk, and godly tracts filled out the packs. Few of the old tracts last today. Samuel Pepys bound his best ones into small books with gay names. The text traces the form to French tracts of the late 1400s. Those of the 1700s, it warns, are poor work in both print and prose.
britannica-1911-exeter-book: The Exeter Book, or Codex Exoniensis, is an anthology of Anglo-Saxon poetry. The hosted text says it was presented to Exeter cathedral by Leofric. That is all that survives here. The hosted text is a fragment of 109 bytes that breaks off mid-sentence just after Leofric's name. Nothing of the book's contents, age or later history stands in the hosted text, so none of it is described.
britannica-1911-gartok: Gartok, a trade market of Tibet, is given a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the bank of the Indus, on the road between Shigatse and Leh. Under the Tibet treaty of 1904 it was opened to British trade, with Yatung and Gyantse. A party from the Lhasa column visited that year and found only a few dozen people in winter quarters, in houses amid a bare plain. In summer, though, all the trade between Tibet and Ladakh passes through the place.
britannica-1911-horn-book:
Horn-book, in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, is an article on an early primer used to teach children to read. The horn-book was a sheet with the alphabet, set on wood and covered with clear horn to guard it. Its wooden frame had a handle, and a child often wore it hung at the girdle.

The entry lists what the sheet held, in order. A large cross came first, then the alphabet in large and small letters. Vowels and their blends with consonants followed in table form. An opening prayer, the Lord's Prayer, and Roman numerals closed the page. The article also cites mentions in plays by Shakespeare and Ben Jonson, which show how well known the object once was.
britannica-1911-ingle-nook:
Ingle Nook, the snug seat by a great hearth, is the topic of a brief home craft note in the 1911 Britannica. The word rests on a Latin word for a small fire. The nook sits in the breast of the chimney, by the flame. Wide Tudor hearths could hold a wood bench at each end of the mouth. Those seats sat clear of harsh heat yet close to the glow.

Such seats helped block the drafts that plagued old homes as well. Books and verse of England are full of fond words for the nook. Small grates killed the form in most homes in time. New builders in England and America now add them back in old style homes. Owners of old homes oft tear out grates to bring them back.
britannica-1911-rook:
Rook, a bird of the crow tribe, is the subject of a long study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the most common and best known crow across a great part of Europe. Unlike its kin, it loves company through the year. At an early age it sheds the plumes from its face, which leaves a bare grey-white patch of skin.

Where the face plumes stay, a rich purple gloss marks the bird out from the crow. Rooks nest in groups called rookeries, each with ways of its own. Most British rooks stay put, but many young birds fly south in the fall. In the far north of its range the rook is a bird of summer only. In the warm south it comes for the cold months alone.
britannica-1911-rudok: Rudok is a small town on the Ladakh frontier of Tibet, described in a brief place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. All trade from Tibet to Leh passed through it, and a Chinese outpost there long blocked travel by men from Europe. Houses rise in tiers on a lone hill near Lake Pangong, whitewashed and walled. A large palace and red monasteries crown the hill. The town stands about thirteen thousand feet above the sea, with dry winter air and light snow.
britannica-1911-taylor-brook:
Brook Taylor, an English mathematician, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Edmonton in Middlesex in sixteen eighty five, he was the son of John Taylor of Bifrons House in Kent. He entered Saint John's College, Cambridge, in seventeen hundred one. He took law degrees there in the years that followed.

He had studied maths under John Machin and John Keill at Cambridge. In seventeen hundred eight he found a striking solution to a problem on the centre of oscillation. That work stayed unpublished for six years. When it did appear, his claim to be first was disputed. The entry follows that dispute and his later work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-domesday-book:
Domesday Book records the great survey of England that William the Conqueror ordered in 1085 and 1086. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains the name, first found in the Dialogue of the Exchequer about 1176. The English called the survey Domesday, or Day of Judgment, because no holding escaped its inquiry and its verdict on land was final, without appeal.

Native chroniclers resented the inquisition, with one writing that no ox, cow, or swine was left unrecorded. The returns tell who held each parcel in 1085 and in King Edward's time, with its size, nature, and value. The entry points students to Maitland, Round, and Ballard among modern guides to this foundation stone of English history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-przemysl-samb:
This encyclopedia entry treats a Greek Catholic diocese of Western Galicia, in Austria, under its triple name. In truth it is the Diocese of Przemysl of the Greek Rite. Sambor marks only an old contest between Catholics and Orthodox at the time of the churches' union. Sanok never held a bishopric at all. Przemysl itself, a fortified town on the River San, lies fifty-four miles west of Lemberg.

In 1900 it counted 46,350 people, and it held the Cathedral of the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist with the diocesan seminary of the Ruthenian Greek Catholics. Sambor, a manufacturing town on the Dniester ten miles away, counted some 17,350 people in 1900. Sanok, smaller still, lay on the San about twenty-five miles to the south-west. Sources from Lemberg and Vienna histories to the 1910 diocesan directory round out a compact portrait of a borderland church.
child-s-first-picture-book: Anonymous picture-book pages pair each bold illustration with a few plain lines for a very young reader. Fire horses wait in their stalls and rush to the engine at the gong. A motor fire engine, a brave fireman, a hose nozzle on a roof, and the firemen's dog fill the first half. Trains take over next: a roundhouse turntable, a water tank, an observation train following college boat races, a train ferry, and a stage coach. The hosted text is only the captions, short and simple throughout.
doe-osti-2588955-infrared-thermometer-in:
Josh Howie, Victor Morris, and Lexie Goldberger of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory wrote this instrument handbook, DOE/SC-ARM-TR-015, dated September 2025, for the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement user facility. It documents the infrared thermometer, the IRT: a downward-looking radiometer that measures the surface's skin temperature without touching it, a key input for energy balance studies.

Handbooks in this series are the operating reference for an instrument across all ARM sites. This one covers the hardware and its data acquisition wiring, data quality procedures, and the datastreams the instrument produces. The main product, gndirt, reports upwelling, one-minute-averaged surface temperature at most mobile facilities and fixed sites. Taller installations add streams from 10 meters at the Southern Great Plains site only, and from 25 meters. Users learn here exactly what those numbers mean and how much to trust them.
doe-osti-2997625-efficiency-project-play:
Los Alamos National Laboratory playbook LA-UR-25-29838, by Justin Scott, issued 2 October 2025, is a how-to manual for running efficiency improvement projects at the laboratory. It walks a project from first scoping to a decisional brief a manager can approve or reject. Templates carry much of the method, so teams do not invent their own paperwork each time.

Scoping comes first: name the exact areas, processes, or departments in play, and tie the effort to laboratory goals. Two starter documents anchor the phase, a Project Plan Overview that sequences the path to a decision, and a Project Charter that fixes what must be decided. Later sections supply templates through a PowerPoint decisional brief and a roles and responsibilities table. The playbook standardizes how improvement ideas become funded, bounded projects.
doe-osti-3376012-cyber-informed-engineer:
An Idaho National Laboratory workbook dated December 2025, by Benjamin Lampe and Virginia Wright, applies cyber-informed engineering to the radio link between the two ends of a freight train. The head-of-train unit sits with the crew. The end-of-train device rides the last car and reports brake pipe pressure and motion. The link runs on the IEEE 802.16t specification. If the link is spoofed or jammed, the crew can lose sight of the train's tail.

The workbook walks analysts through the CIE principles one by one, as questions. Principle eleven covers control of engineering facts: who holds the plans, and how they leak. Job ads and bid packs can hand a foe the map of a system's weak spots. Each principle pairs such prompts with space to log the design choices they force. The aim is gear that stays safe even when its network does not.
doe-osti-3630799-power-lane-county-elect:
Pacific Northwest report PNNL-39164, the Power Lane County Electric Grid Handbook, reached its second draft in May 2026 and print in July 2026. Ali Trueworthy, Ian Hermanson, Brooke Marten, and Michael Barthelmes edited and assembled it. Lane County, Oregon joined the Energy to Communities program in 2024. Lab help over three years comes from Berkeley, Pacific Northwest, and Rockies staff, with local utility partners.

The handbook gives county staff and the public a base view of the local electric system. Part one explains how power works, who runs it, and how the county system grew. Later parts draw on public data and on interviews with utilities and local groups. The aim is cheaper, more reliable, and tougher service as hazards and loads rise. It closes with a review of project openings found for the county. Nine chapters in all build that shared starting point for talks and later analysis.
favorite-dishes-a-columbian-autograph-so:
Carrie V. Shuman's Favorite Dishes is a Columbian souvenir cookery book. It holds over three hundred autograph recipes, with twenty-three portraits. The recipes were sent in by the World's Columbian Exposition lady managers. Shuman compiled the Chicago volume to help women raise the funds for a visit to the Exposition.

Lady Managers and Lady Alternates from every state and territory sent their own favourite recipes. Alaska was included too, so the book reads as a national album of domestic cookery as much as a manual. Soups, meats, cakes and preserves sit beside the signatures and faces of the women who chose them. Cooks and historians alike will enjoy it as a window onto what accomplished American hostesses actually served in 1893.
flying-machines-construction-and-operati:
W J Jackman and Thomas H Russell wrote Flying Machines: Construction and Operation in 1912 for the novice who wanted to build and navigate the modern aeroplane. Octave Chanute, president of the Aero Club of Illinois and a pioneer glider experimenter, supplied an introductory chapter. The preface promises practical guidance on theory, construction, and operation.

Early chapters trace the two-surface machine from Chanute and the Wrights, compare helicopters, ornithopters, and monoplanes, and give plans for a gliding machine with costs and materials. Later discussion works out wing-tip control by varying surface area at the extremities. Published when flying was still a workshop hobby, the book captures aviation at its most experimental and hopeful.
govdocs-archive_org-mazdean-critique-of-:
The Shkand-Gumanig Vizar, the Doubt-Dispelling Exposition, is a ninth-century Zoroastrian defense of the faith written by Mardanfarrokh, son of Hurmazddad. He wrote in Persia, in a land already ruled by Islam for two centuries, to answer doubts among his fellow Zoroastrians.

The work reasons through God's goodness, the origin of evil, and the claims of rival faiths, including a direct critique of Islam. It is one of the richest surviving works of Zoroastrian theology. One caution: the text in this copy is corrupted by a character-encoding shift, which garbles the reading in places.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CookBook_Cook_B: A promotional flyer from the Delmarva Poultry Industry, Inc. announces the finals of the National Chicken Cooking Contest. The sheet was made to publicize the contest's final round, in which home cooks competed with chicken dishes. Nothing in the surviving record gives the flyer's date or names the finalists, so it stands mainly as a piece of poultry industry publicity from the contest era.
govdocs-archive_org-phantom-gerhard-haup:
Gerhart Hauptmann won the Nobel Prize in Literature, and his 1922 novel Phantom shows his darker side at full strength. Bayard Quincy Morgan translated it into English. The story follows a minor clerk who becomes obsessed with a strange young woman he barely knows.

Hauptmann mixes crime, longing, and mirage as the clerk's fixation pulls his whole life apart, page by page. The novel reads partly as confession and partly as fever dream. It stands as a German classic of the years after the First World War, when many writers were drawn to minds coming loose from ordinary life.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia_The_Bolton_B:
John Bolton, Donald Trump's former national security adviser, wrote a memoir called The Room Where It Happened. In June 2020 the Trump administration went to court to try to stop it. A National Security Archive posting from June 19, 2020 covers that fight and places it in a longer line of cases over officials publishing what the government calls classified secrets.

The posting includes documentation of earlier prepublication review cases, the system under which former officials must clear manuscripts before printing. That history is the Archive's contribution: book fights look new each time, but the review machinery is old and its rules shape what the public learns. Readers get both the breaking story of one famous memoir and the background needed to judge the censorship claim behind it.
jewel-s-story-book:
Clara Louise Burnham published Jewel's Story Book at New York in 1904, for the children who love Jewel. Mrs. Forbes answers the telephone as Mr. Evringham asks for Jewel in the first chapter. Contents promise a quest flower, an apple woman's story, and a golden dog. A talking doll and Robinson Crusoe follow.

Gabriel risks prison by accusing an organ-grinder, in one tale inside the book. He had seen the brown dog's eyes, and his heart bounded with certainty. A princess bids her waiting man stand back during the farce-like trial. Jewel's circle hears stories of faith, kindness, and true delight.
leaves-from-a-field-note-book:
J. H. Morgan wrote Leaves from a Field Note-Book from his war service. He had served as a Home Office commissioner with the British Expeditionary Force. Macmillan published the book in London and New York.

A field note-book suggests scenes set down near the events themselves. Morgan records soldiers, places, and moments from the front. His motto comes from Proverbs: his delights were with the sons of men. That warmth suits a book of observed human detail. Readers get a staff officer's eye joined to a humane pen. Morgan's official role let him see the war's machinery closely. His notes balance that wide view with small human scenes.
mary-jane-her-book:
Clara Ingram Judson wrote Mary Jane: Her Book for young children. Short chapters follow one small girl through her days at home. The contents list names each small event in plain words.

Mary Jane breaks a doll, spills sugar, and helps the robins. She plays school, learns to sew, and plans a picnic up Clearwater. A birthday party, a letter, and a trip close the book. Each tale turns a small mishap into a kind lesson. Father's secret and a paper doll show add small home drama. Judson keeps each scene short, plain, and close to a child's scale.
mcguffey-s-eclectic-spelling-book:
Alexander H. McGuffey's Eclectic Spelling Book appears here in revised form. A front note asks if readers can still spell pharmacopoeia. Hard words like that were set for sixth grade pupils.

The preface says the book keeps the strengths of the old speller. Webster's marks for sounds replace the old number code. Lessons teach prefixes and suffixes near the end of the book. Pupils learn by rules of sound and sense, not by rote alone. Lessons on each sound mark come early, in drills 36 to 57. Sound, sense, and accent work as one in the plan.
miss-parloa-s-new-cook-book:
Maria Parloa, principal of the School of Cooking in Boston, wrote this guide to marketing and cooking. Her preface explains her method. After seeing many failures in home kitchens, she resolved to give minute directions for everything. Little is left to the cook's judgment, on purpose.

The chapter on marketing teaches buyers to choose meats, fish, and vegetables intelligently. Hundreds of recipes follow, nearly all prepared especially for this book. Soups, salads, entrées, and desserts receive unusual length. Parloa argues that those dishes make a table healthful, economical, and elegant. Her book brought cooking-school standards into ordinary American homes.
nasa-tm-19660025355-failure-information-:
Issued on March 1, 1966, the Failure Information Notebook came from the Quality and Reliability Assurance Laboratory. That laboratory sits at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama. Numbered SR-QUAL-66-4, it gathers recorded failure information for major parts of the Saturn I launch vehicle and its ground support equipment.

Inside, components from the electrical, electromechanical, and mechanical systems are cataloged with their running times and cycle counts. Qualification test results sit beside failure categories, failure frequencies, and failure rates. Observed mean time before failure is given for each part, and an index lets engineers compare past performance quickly. The notebook was built as a shared reference for judging reliability and predicting how parts would perform in the future.
phebe-her-profession-a-sequel-to-teddy-h:
Anna Chapin Ray's Phebe, Her Profession, a sequel to Teddy: Her Book, is dated 1902. It opens in Helena, where a young man sunk in a brown study is hailed by a small boy. The cherub, clutching a paper bag of candy and a rusty hoop, asks politely how everybody is at his house.

The boy has been kept from walking alone for almost a month for spending his pennies at Jake's candy shop. Charmed, the stranger falls into talk with him. Ray builds her story of Phebe and her circle from such small encounters, in the bright manner of her girls' books.
podcast-dannyjones-uQPAVic3Jok:
Researcher Carl Hayden Smith joins Danny Jones to tell how he was injected with DMT so teams could study the fabric of reality. Smith works on how tech and drugs shift the sense of self. He speaks as a test subject here.

Smith tells what the drug showed him, step by step, under lab watch. He talks about the beings, the sense of a built world, and what stayed with him after. Jones asks how a lab can use such wild reports as data. Listeners get a rare first hand lab tale. The library holds the talk as an archive record of his account.
podcast-joerogan-zv8pjyJH4Ok:
Dr. Gabor Mate talks trauma and healing with Joe Rogan in episode 1869 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Mate, a Canadian physician, argues that addiction and many illnesses grow out of early wounds. His book The Myth of Normal questions what modern life does to body and mind.

Mate explains his method of compassionate inquiry, asking patients what happened to them rather than what is wrong with them. He shares stories from his work with addicts in Vancouver's hardest streets. Rogan asks about his own habits and stresses under that lens. The talk offers a gentle, searching view of pain and recovery.
podcast-tuckercarlson-HzHSK7WXqok:
A Gold Star father joins Tucker Carlson to accuse the Biden team of shameful conduct. His son died in service, and grief fuels every word. His quote gives the episode its title: we were used.

He describes the return of the fallen and the words of officials. He says leaders staged honor while dodging blame for a failed exit. Carlson lets the father's anger run without softening it. The episode honors the dead through a parent's charge. It will hit hardest with military families who feel their loss was mishandled.
putnam-s-word-book:
Putnam's Word Book, by Louis A. Flemming, is a writer's aid to an exact and varied vocabulary, copyrighted in 1913 by G. P. Putnam's Sons. It first appeared under the title Synonyms, Antonyms, and Associated Words, and its lists group words with their near matches and related terms.

A long list of short forms opens the book. It marks parts of speech. It names fields such as botany, chemistry, medicine, and music. It also gives the source tongues of words, from French and German to Hebrew and Spanish. A note adds that further words, with their synonyms, stand in an addenda that begins on page 615.
sleep-book:
Leolyn Louise Everett gathered Sleep-Book, subtitled Some of the Poetry of Slumber, printed at New York by the Watkins Company in 1910. Only three hundred and twenty copies were made, on hand-made Van Gelder paper. Everett gives the book to Ethel Du Fré Houston, who, she says, brought the joy and beauty of dream into many lives.

The first piece, signed by Everett, speaks straight to a restless heart. It bids the heart be still, tells the soul to drop the cares and stir of the day, and asks night to take the sleeper into her own calm. A second piece then hails sleep as a soft-breathing god whose downy wing flutters near.
the-1990-cia-world-factbook: The World Factbook 1990 was made each year by the Central Intelligence Agency. It was made for the use of United States government staff. Its style and scope were shaped to their needs. This copy is the electronic form. Its contents list runs to 249 entries. Nations, dependent areas, and other entities fill the list. It runs from Afghanistan and Albania onward. Oceans and polar lands stand in the same roll.
the-1991-cia-world-factbook: The CIA World Factbook 1991 is dated October 15, 1991. Search tags open the copy. They mark country names and section heads. Geography, People, Government, and Economy are the heads named. Single facts gain marks of their own. A front note states the book's source. The Central Intelligence Agency makes it each year. It is made for United States government staff. Facts came from the Bureau of the Census and the Defense Intelligence Agency. The Department of State and other named sources helped as well.
the-1992-cia-world-factbook:
The CIA World Factbook 1992 appears here in a Project Gutenberg printing dated January 1, 1993, set in plain ASCII with search marks for each land and topic. A front note explains how to find a country and each of its sections, from Geography to Defense Forces.

Entries then start with Afghanistan, whose geography is given in full. Its total area is 647,500 square kilometers, a bit smaller than Texas, with 5,529 kilometers of land borders and no coastline at all. Disputes noted include the Pashtunistan issue with Pakistan. Readers get a year-by-year snapshot of every land on earth, in fixed fields that make lands easy to compare.
the-1993-cia-world-factbook: The 1993 CIA World Factbook stands here in a first, rough Gutenberg form. A note flags it as a preliminary edition. A final one was due near midnight on October 31, 1993. The front pages explain search marks for lands and topics. Geography, People, Government, and Economy are the topics named. A contents roll then follows. It runs from Afghanistan onward. New names such as Armenia and Azerbaijan stand in the roll.
the-1994-cia-world-factbook: The 1994 CIA World Factbook opens with search help. An at-sign mark finds each land and topic. Geography, People, Government, and Economy are named. Communications and Defense Forces are named as well. The front pages give copy routes for staff. United States government staff should get copies through their own groups. Sale routes are also listed. They run through the Superintendent of Documents. They run through the Library of Congress DOCEX project. They run through the National Technical Information Service as well.
the-1995-cia-world-factbook: The 1995 CIA World Factbook opens with search help. At-sign marks find each land and topic. Transportation now stands in the topic list. Contents run from publication facts first. Notes on terms and short forms come next. An A-to-Z roll of lands then follows. It starts with Afghanistan. It runs through the Bahamas, Bahrain, and Bosnia and Herzegovina.
the-1997-cia-world-factbook: The 1997 CIA World Factbook opens with a contents list. An introduction comes first. A brief history of basic intelligence and the Factbook follows. Notes and definitions come next. A guide to country profiles follows them. It sets out classes, fields, and subfields. The A-to-Z roll of lands then starts. Afghanistan, Albania, and Algeria head the roll.
the-1998-cia-world-factbook: Dr. Gregory B. Newby prepared the CIA World Factbook 1998 for Project Gutenberg. He took it from the CIA's online version of the book. His note warns that maps are not included. Other graphics from the source are left out as well. Tables may not align well after conversion. They are otherwise intact, he says. The CIA does not keep past Factbooks online. This saved copy may thus serve readers for years.
the-2000-cia-world-factbook: Martin M. Pedersen prepared the CIA World Factbook 2000. He took it from the CIA's online version of the book. His note warns that maps are left out. Graphics are left out as well. Tables may not align after conversion. The CIA does not keep past Factbooks online, he notes. A contents list then follows. It rolls from Afghanistan onward in A-to-Z order. Notes and appendixes follow the country listings.
the-2002-cia-world-factbook: The CIA World Factbook 2002 heads its copy as a country listing. Lands then roll past in A-to-Z order. Afghanistan, Albania, and Algeria come first. The roll runs on through Cambodia and beyond. Oceans stand in the same roll. Polar lands stand there too. Small island areas are mixed in with the rest.
the-belgian-cookbook:
Mrs Brian Luck edited a cookery book in 1915 from recipes sent by Belgian refugees across the United Kingdom. A preface says British cooking may gain from Belgian dishes. The book is aimed at working mistresses and maids, not at millionaires, and most recipes are simple and cheap.

Advice opens each course. Savouries should be small, neat, and alluring, like an ankle. Soup must be very hot and have a good foundation, not a pot of warm water with a cow driven past the door. Fish must be truly fresh, the editor insists, not kept from Saturday to Monday on a false hope.
the-blotting-book:
E. F. Benson published a novel in 1908 that opens on a house of perfect order in Sussex Square, Brighton. Mrs Assheton's rooms are never too hot or cold, meals are always on time, and her Scotch cook never serves a poor dish. Parlour-maids meet guests' wants before they are spoken.

Silver shines, carpets are soft, a billiard table is free of dust, and cigarette boxes stay full. Mrs Assheton, widowed and living alone until her son Morris returned from four years at Cambridge three months earlier, keeps every ceremony even when dining alone. Such smooth formality, presented as self-respect, begs for a crack to appear.
the-blue-fairy-book: Andrew Lang edited The Blue Fairy Book, a large set of folk and fairy tales by many hands. The list of tales runs to more than thirty stories. It holds Little Red Riding-Hood, Cinderella, and the Sleeping Beauty in the Wood. It also holds Aladdin, Beauty and the Beast, Puss in Boots, and Hansel and Gretel. Jack the Giant-Killer, the Forty Thieves, and Blue Beard are there too. The first tale named is The Bronze Ring, though none of the tales is printed in full here.
the-blue-jar-story-book:
The Blue Jar Story Book, dated 1906 from McLoughlin Brothers of New York, holds tales by Maria Edgeworth, Charles Lamb, Mary Lamb, and Alicia Catherine Mant. Its list names six tales in all. They are The Blue Jar, The Basket Woman, The Sea Voyage, The Changeling, The Inquisitive Girl, and The Little Blue Bag.

Edgeworth's title tale starts in London, where a girl of about seven named Rosamond walks with her mother past shop fronts. She sees goods whose names and uses she does not know, and she longs to stop and look. She tells her mother she would be glad to have all the fine things in a toy shop, and her mother asks if she wants them all. The scene sets up a child's wish for more than she needs.
the-bobbsey-twins-at-meadow-brook: Laura Lee Hope wrote The Bobbsey Twins at Meadow Brook, one of her tales of the four Bobbsey young folk. The part names trace a summer stay from a crash of dishes and new plans to a runaway boy and the trip out. Snap's Escape, At Meadow Brook, The Picnic, and Lost in the Hay come next. A sham fight, films, the twins on stage, and a circus crowd the mid parts. Late parts bring Freddie lost and found, Frank's tale, a wild beast scare, a swim, and bad cash.
the-crimson-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang edited The Crimson Fairy Book, written by various hands. His preface admits that each fairy book demands a preface from its editor, and that such pieces are unavoidably dull and useless. Honesty, he says, forces him to keep repeating that he is the editor, not the author, of the tales.

Lang compares his role to that of a man of science toward nature: popular tales are too vast to be the work of one modern mind. The editor's business is to hunt for tales told by peasant or savage grandmothers in many lands, from New Caledonia to Zululand, from polar snows to Greece, Spain, Italy, and far Lochaber.
the-firelight-fairy-book:
Henry Beston wrote The Firelight Fairy Book for young readers, with pictures by Maurice E. Day, printed at Boston in 1919. A short word list at the front explains hard terms like halberd and seneschal.

Beston retells old fairy tales in a warm, fireside voice, keeping the odd speech and dress of the source tales. Kings, guards, spells, and quests fill the pages, with the meanings of strange words set out plainly for children. The book treats fairy lore as a living store of wonder, to be read aloud while the fire burns low and the room grows dark.
the-golden-goose-book:
L. Leslie Brooke made The Golden Goose Book. Frederick Warne and Company printed it in London. It was first printed in 1905. It has many drawings in colour and black and white. The book holds four tales. They are The Golden Goose, The Three Bears, The Three Little Pigs, and Tom Thumb.

The first tale begins in the classic way. A man had three sons. The youngest was called the Simpleton. He was laughed at, scorned, and neglected on all occasions. One day the eldest son wanted to go into the wood. The tale moves off from there. Brooke's retellings keep the old plots. They add his pictures. Those pictures made the book a nursery favourite for young children.
the-green-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang edited The Green Fairy Book. The tales are by various hands. The book is dedicated to Stella Margaret Alleyne. It comes third in the series of Fairy Books of many colours, after the Blue and the Red, and Lang expects it to close the set. Its stories come from many lands: France, Germany, Russia, and Italy all supply some, Scotland and England others, and China one.

The preface argues that tales of this kind are the oldest in the world. Early men, childlike in mind, told each other such stories long before newspapers or novels existed. Grandmothers handed them down to grandchildren. The first ever set down in writing were Egyptian, from near Joseph's time, some three thousand five hundred years ago. Homer shaped tales of the same kind into the Odyssey.
the-grey-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang edited The Grey Fairy Book. The tales are by various hands. His preface says the tales come from many countries. They come from Lithuania and parts of Africa. They come from Germany, France, Greece, and other regions. One tale, The Three Sons of Hali, comes from the old French Cabinet des Fees. It puts tale within tale, like the Eastern balls of carved ivory.

The contents name twenty tales. They open with Donkey Skin and The Goblin Pony. They name The Story of Dschemil and Dachemila, Fortunatus and His Purse, and The Goat-faced Girl. They name The Magician's Horse, The Little Gray Man, and Udea and Her Seven Brothers. They name The White Wolf, Bobino, and The Dog and the Sparrow. The preface argues that popular fiction shakes a fixed stock of incidents into new combinations, like the glass in a kaleidoscope.
the-illustrated-london-reading-book:
The Illustrated London News published this reading book in 1851. Its office stood at 198 Strand. This copy is the third edition. Additions and corrections mark it. The introduction opens with verses on reading well. Few men read or speak with true feeling, they say. The design of the book follows plainly. It aims to strip lessons of their terrors. It strews flowers on the paths to knowledge.

Young readers were to find masterworks inside. Prose and verse from English letters fill the pages. Pictures run throughout the book. A frontispiece shows Prince Albert in his Cambridge robes. He wears the dress of the university's chancellor. The publishers were famous for their pictured newspaper. They brought the same approach to schooling. Drill alone was not their aim. They wanted to charm and move young readers too.
the-kiltartan-history-book: Lady Gregory wrote this history of Ireland in her Kiltartan manner, illustrated by Robert Gregory and aimed at the new university's history classes. Only the title pages and contents are present here. The text itself does not appear. The contents retell the whole sweep in folk style. Ancient times and Goban the builder open them. The Danes and the Battle of Clontarf follow. The English, Henry VIII, and Elizabeth come next. Cromwell's trace and the Battle of Aughrim appear. Patrick Sarsfield, Carolan's song, and Ninety-Eight close the list.
the-lady-of-the-aroostook:
William Dean Howells opens this novel in a farmhouse's best room. Three people sit one August morning in unaccustomed finery. The elderly mother rocks in the haircloth armchair. She calls her husband father. He drums noiseless fingers on the table. His lips pucker to a whistle that makes no sound. His weekly shave leaves frosty stubble in the deeper wrinkles. At the table's other end, their daughter Lyddy leans with face averted. She stares at the hens in the door-yard. She dabs her eyes.

The parents debate the parting in dialect. The mother does not want Lyddy to go. Keeping her home would cost no more than sending her, she says. The father thinks he might recover some passage money. The captain did not seem grasping, he notes. Howells builds his tale from this grief. A country girl voyages to Trieste.
the-lilac-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang edited this fairy tale collection and filled its preface with dinner party complaints. Strangers, he says, always ask a writer what he is writing now. One lady asked if he ever wrote anything but fairy books, and a French expert printed the same claim in a newspaper.

Lang jokes that he should claim a grave treatise on potato blight instead of answering. Behind the teasing stands a serious gatherer of tales from many lands. The lilac volume closes his color fairy book series, drawing stories from Portuguese, Irish, Welsh, and other sources for child and adult readers.
the-little-tea-book:
Arthur Gray compiled The Little Tea Book, published by the Baker and Taylor Company in New York in 1903 with illustrations by George W. Hood. Gray had earlier compiled Over the Black Coffee, and this small volume does the same service for tea. Its introduction declares that tea is the drink of the world, domestically and socially, whatever statistics say about other crops.

Gray argues that no other product has been held in such high regard by writers of standing and good taste. A glance through the book, he says, shows the spirit of tea as one of peace, comfort, and refinement. Readers get a light anthology of tea praise, quotation, and lore, opened by a verse tribute from Colley Cibber.
the-moral-picture-book:
The Moral Picture Book opens with a story headed John Cooper, illustrated with scenes captioned Prayer and Affection. John Cooper, an only child living with his parents in a cottage beside a village green, owns a dog named Carlo whom he loves. His playmate Tom Jones tempts him into truancy one school day.

Tom proposes a long walk along the stream instead of lessons, hunting birds' nests in the wood. Sunshine, full leaves, butterflies, and singing birds make the outing look joyful. Only Carlo is truly happy, the narrator insists. John cannot forget he has done wrong and will grieve his kind parents, while Tom laughs loudly to smother his own bitter feelings. A mile into the wood, the boys spot a wren's nest in an old willow.
the-new-dr-price-cookbook:
The New Dr. Price Cook Book, issued for use with Dr. Price's Phosphate Baking Powder from the Price Baking Powder Factory in Chicago, is present here only in a publisher's introduction and the start of an index, so no recipes appear. The Royal Baking Powder Company held the 1921 copyright. Recipes of universal appeal, the introduction promises, were chosen to be popular in every home and useful every day of the year.

Famous recipes were made more appealing with the baking powder, the note says, while economising on eggs and other costly ingredients. New recipes were meant to suit beginners yet earn laurels for experts. The index begins with Albuminized Orange, salted almonds, Angel Cake, and apple dishes.
the-ontario-readers-fourth-book: The Ontario Readers, Fourth Book, was a school reader authorized by the Minister of Education for Ontario and entered in Canada in 1909, published by the T. Eaton Company of Toronto. The title page and the start of a contents list are present, and no lesson text follows them. The contents open with Kipling's Children's Song and Tennyson's Our Country, and list pieces by George Eliot, Shakespeare, Christina Rossetti, Stevenson, Parkman, Dickens, and the Bible.
the-ontario-readers-third-book: The Ontario Readers, Third Book, was a school reader authorized by the Minister of Education for Ontario and entered in Canada in 1909, published in Toronto by the T. Eaton Company. Only the front matter is present here, chiefly lists of thanks for permission to reprint, so the lessons themselves do not appear. The Minister thanks Kipling, Henry Newbolt, Flora Annie Steel, Charles G. D. Roberts, and Ralph Connor, among many others. A frontispiece shows the Union Jack.
the-pink-fairy-book:
The Pink Fairy Book, edited by Andrew Lang, gathers nursery tales from many parts of the world. Lang's preface observes that Japanese, Chinese, Native American, Eskimo, African, Greek, and Egyptian tellers all hand such tales to their children. The stories often resemble one another across great distances. Readers of the earlier Blue, Red, and Yellow Fairy Books will meet old friends with new faces here. They will also meet figures new to them, such as the Japanese Tanuki.

Lang names the helpers behind the volume. W. A. Craigie translated the Danish and Swedish tales. Mrs. Lang rendered the Sicilian, African, Catalan, Japanese, and old French stories through German and French versions. Alma Alleyne took the Andersen tales from the German.
